title: Dragon Ball Goku voice actor furious at “unforgivable” AI videos using her voice: “It has no heart”
summary: Dragon Ball voice actress Masako Nozawa has slammed AI-generated videos using her voice without permission.
details: Trending GTA 6 Modern Warfare 4 Twitch EA FC 27 Wardogs TV & Movies Anime Dragon Ball Goku voice actor furious at “unforgivable” AI videos using her voice: “It has no heart” by Michael Gwilliam Published: Oct 15, 2026, 17:53 Save for later Save for later NHK/Toei Add as a preferred source on Google Follow on Google News Dragon Ball voice actress Masako Nozawa has slammed AI-generated videos using her voice without permission, calling the practice “unforgivable” and comparing it to theft. The 89-year-old Japanese actress has voiced Goku since Dragon Ball debuted in 1986, also portraying characters including Gohan and Goten throughout the franchise. Her decades of work have earned her widespread recognition, with Nozawa becoming the first voice actor to receive one of Japan’s highest cultural honors in 2025. However, the Dragon Ball legend is now speaking out against the growing use of artificial intelligence to recreate her performances without consent. Article continues after ad Crunchyroll Goku voice actress blasts AI videos for stealing her voice Speaking to Japanese broadcaster NHK , Nozawa expressed her frustration with AI-generated videos that imitate her voice, arguing that the technology cannot replicate the emotion behind her performances. “It has no heart,” she said, according to a translation shared by Dragon Ball Hype. “It might even be a perfect copy. But it has no heart, does it? Without heart, it’s no good, whatever the role. Even a voice that’s only crying is different when you cry with real feeling. That’s what I believe.” Article continues after ad Article continues after ad “This is not my voice. Using it without permission is unforgivable. It’s the same as theft, and it makes me angry,” she added. Nozawa stressed that her voice and acting belong to her, arguing that anyone looking to recreate or use her performances should seek permission first. Masako Nozawa comments on the use of generative AI in voice acting: "I can't forgive using it without asking. I want people to follow the rules.” After watching AI videos of her voice: "This is not my voice. Using it without asking is unforgivable. It's the same as stealing,… pic.twitter.com/o3w5F1rBeK — Hype (@DbsHype) October 15, 2026 The comments came as the Japan Actors Union, which represents roughly 2,600 actors and voice performers, announced new guidelines on October 15 aimed at protecting performers from unauthorized AI voice cloning. Related Genshin Impact dev wins over $100K after AI company cloned character voices Evangelion star calls for Japanese government help over “heartbreaking” AI voice cloning Goku voice actor accuses popular Dragon Ball YouTuber of using AI to fake voices Article continues after ad The guidelines call for performers to give consent before their voices are used to train AI models, generate new recordings, or appear in published content. They also outline appropriate compensation and protections against unauthorized use. Nozawa is not entirely opposed to the technology, however. In a video message supporting the announcement, she expressed excitement about AI’s potential while criticizing those using performers’ voices without permission. She’s far from the only anime star raising concerns about the growing technology. Article continues after ad Article continues after ad In August 2026, Evangelion voice actress Megumi Ogata called AI voice cloning “heartbreaking” and urged Japan’s government to intervene. Meanwhile, Goku’s English voice actor Sean Schemmel previously accused a popular Dragon Ball YouTuber of using AI to imitate his voice , although the creator denied the allegations and insisted the impressions were entirely his own. With AI-generated anime content becoming increasingly widespread, Nozawa’s comments highlight the growing concerns among voice actors about losing control of the characters and performances they’ve spent decades bringing to life. title: My Dress-Up Darling gets life-size Marin Kitagawa figure with $8,000 price tag
summary: My Dress-Up Darling fans can now pre-order a life-size Marin Kitagawa figure, but the popular anime girl will set you back a whopping $8,000.
details: Trending GTA 6 Modern Warfare 4 Twitch EA FC 27 Wardogs Entertainment My Dress-Up Darling gets life-size Marin Kitagawa figure with $8,000 price tag by James Busby Save for later Save for later Prime 1 Studio Add as a preferred source on Google Follow on Google News Last updated on October 23, 2026 My Dress-Up Darling fans can now pre-order a life-size Marin Kitagawa figure, but the popular anime girl will set you back a whopping $8,000. It’s been a big year for My Dress-Up Darling’s best girl, Marin Kitagawa. The cosplay-loving anime girl has appeared on everything from professional race cars to giant plushies that weigh as much as a small dog . In a move that will undoubtedly have your friends and family asking questions when they enter your living room, Marin fans can now pick up a life-size figure that comes with a lot of detail and a hefty price tag. Article continues after ad Massive Marin Kitagawa figure is up for pre-order The handmade figure stands approximately 5 feet 5 inches tall and weighs 17.6 pounds, and comes kitted out in her school uniform. Unlike Date A Live’s life-size Kurumi Tokisaki and Ghost in the Shell’s massive Motoko Kusanagi statue , Marin comes with two swappable left arms. This means fans can switch between her signature peace sign and open-hand pose, depending on which you prefer. Prime 1 Studio has also revealed that her fabric school uniform shirt, necktie, and skirt have been adjusted to recreate her outfit’s relaxed look from the anime. Article continues after ad Article continues after ad Marin’s swimsuit from Season 1 also makes an appearance, recreating the look that famously left cosplayer craftsman Gojo flustered. Even little details like Marin’s nails have a glittery look to them, while her hair has been sculpted to give it “a delicate sense of flow”. It certainly looks incredibly realistic, but owning your own hyper-realistic Marin Kitagawa doesn’t come cheap. In fact, you may need to start taking cosplay commissions yourself if you wish to afford the $7,999 price tag. title: Man says he used technique from Detective Conan to save his life after car plunged into river
summary: A man claims he survived a car accident by remembering a technique from Detective Conan, which showed him how to escape a sinking vehicle.
details: Trending GTA 6 Modern Warfare 4 Twitch EA FC 27 Wardogs TV & Movies Anime Man says he used technique from Detective Conan to save his life after car plunged into river by Michael Gwilliam Published: Nov 09, 2026, 16:56 Save for later Save for later X/nozinozi053/Crunchyroll Add as a preferred source on Google Follow on Google News A man in Japan claims he survived a terrifying car accident by remembering a technique from the anime Detective Conan, which showed him how to escape a sinking vehicle. The driver, who posts on X as nozinozi053, revealed on November 8 that his car had ended up in a river following a collision with another motorist. According to his account, the other driver had been reversing near a cemetery when they suddenly pulled forward as he attempted to pass, resulting in a collision. Article continues after ad With his vehicle submerged, the man initially believed he was going to die. However, a scene from Detective Conan suddenly came to mind. “For the first 20 seconds or so, I really thought I was going to die,” he wrote. “But then this scene suddenly flashed through my mind, and I managed to escape alive.” “I can’t thank the creator of Conan enough!” これが、水没してる時に頭をよぎって、生きて脱出出来ました！コナンの作者には感謝しきれません！ ほんとに最初の20秒くらいで死を覚悟したが、不意にこのシーンが頭を過り、生きて出れました https://t.co/8vsQoZeBY6 pic.twitter.com/TLApBiOzIP — みらじーの (@nozinozi053) November 8, 2026 Detective Conan episode 1078 helped driver escape sinking car The scene comes from episode 1078, titled ‘The Black Organization’s Scheme (Landing),’ which originally aired on April 1, 2023. Article continues after ad Article continues after ad In the episode, FBI agent Andre Camel drives into the ocean while being pursued by the Black Organization. Trapped underwater, he discovers that his car doors won’t open because of the pressure outside. Conan instructs Camel to breathe from an air pocket near the roof until the vehicle fills with enough water for the pressure inside and outside to equalize, allowing him to open the door and escape. The sequence is detailed in the anime’s official episode synopsis . Related TV reporter rescues man from sinking truck while filming the news Simple GTA Online trick lets you stay in water without drowning Kick steamer helps car crash victims after driver runs red light and slams into van Article continues after ad The real-life driver said he recalled the scene while underwater and desperately searched for the door handle. いざという時には、コナンで学べる アニメ第1078話「黒ずくめの謀略（上陸）」 アンドレ・キャメル捜査官が黒ずくめの組織に追い詰められ、車ごと海に落下した後に水没した車内から脱出するエピソード https://t.co/z6eSvjUgPt (2023年4月1日放送回) pic.twitter.com/VGy2solGTN — ジンチュウ (@bakugekidayo15) October 2, 2026 “I pulled on it, and the wall to my right moved a little. I realized it was the door, so I pushed it open with all my strength,” he explained. “It was a little heavy, but it opened relatively easily.” When asked whether the other driver had helped him, he revealed that he hadn’t even seen the person responsible for the collision. Instead, a nearby resident helped him climb onto the riverbank. Article continues after ad Article continues after ad Police, emergency services, and local residents subsequently gathered at the scene. Although the man survived, his car was reportedly written off. In a follow-up post , he also revealed that his jacket had floated away in the river. He had assumed someone would retrieve it, but nobody did, leaving him almost as upset as losing his car. Despite the successful escape, the technique shown in Detective Conan is not the recommended first option for escaping a submerged vehicle. Article continues after ad According to AAA , drivers should immediately unbuckle their seat belts and attempt to escape through a window. Waiting for a vehicle to fill with water is extremely dangerous because pressure may not equalize immediately, leaving occupants at risk of drowning. title: Noodle’s 24: Unstaffed make-your-own instant ramen stand is Harajuku’s newest hidden gem
summary: How to eat cheap and try new ramen varieties at this “Self Noodle Shop” in Tokyo. If you’re looking to discover the latest trends in Tokyo, Harajuku needs to be at the top of your list. Not only is it a famous hub for teenagers and cosplayers with their finger on the pulse for all […]
details: How to eat cheap and try new ramen varieties at this “Self Noodle Shop” in Tokyo. If you’re looking to discover the latest trends in Tokyo, Harajuku needs to be at the top of your list. Not only is it a famous hub for teenagers and cosplayers with their finger on the pulse for all things kawaii, it’s also an exciting destination for anyone on the hunt for new food discoveries, as our reporter Mr Sato found when he stumbled across a new store in the area just the other day. Called Noodle’s 24 , this new joint is an unstaffed instant ramen shop where customers can pick out a pack of noodles, add toppings and prepare it all themselves. Originally hailing from South Korea, Noodle’s 24 is all about convenience – it even bills itself as a “ramen convenience store” – and it currently has two branches in Tokyo, one in Harajuku , which opened on 22 October, and one in Asakusa , which opened on 31 October. ▼ With no staff on site, everything is self-service, from payment and cooking through to clean-up afterwards. ▼ Inside, you’ll find shelves filled with packets of Japanese and Korean instant noodles. The Japanese selection includes familiar favourites like Sapporo Ichiban Shio Ramen, Sapporo Ichiban Miso Ramen, Demae Iccho and Maruchan Seimen. All of these are priced at 500 yen (US$3.25). The Korean selection contains 13 varieties, including the popular Shin Ramyun, with prices ranging from 500 to 600 yen. While the noodle selection is impressive, so to are the toppings, as there’s an entire refrigerator stocked full of them. Priced between 100 and 200 yen, some of the options include green onions, corn, kimchi and pork back fat, so you can truly customise your ramen to your liking. To place an order, simply use the tablet terminal near the entrance to select the products you’d like to purchase. There’s no need to scan barcodes, so be careful not to accidentally select the wrong items. When Mr Sato finished making his selections and was ready to pay, a screen appeared asking him to enter the name he’d like to be called. He figured this was so his name could be called out when the order was ready, but that never happened so he’s not entirely sure why it was necessary. ▼ さとう = “Sato” ▼ Payment is cashless only, with various QR code payment services, credit cards and electronic money accepted. After completing his payment, it was time to get cooking. Mr Sato chose something called Sari Gomtang, which had been described on the menu as “a Korean classic”. Looking at the cooking instructions on the back of the packet, he couldn’t understand the Korean writing, but as it was instant ramen, he decided to simply pour the powdered soup over the noodles, as he normally would. After placing the noodles in the special cooking container, he sprinkled the soup powder over them, and then placed the container on the cooking machine and pressed the button marked “Ramen”. ▼ All that was left to do after that was simply wait for the machine to do its thing. Though it might look like the machine simply dispenses hot water, that’s not all it does, as the flat surface is actually an induction heating unit, which helps to heat the noodles. Though Mr Sato initially wondered how the heating element would work with a paper container, it turns out that the base of the bowl is lined with aluminium, allowing heat to be transferred to the noodles inside. ▼ A very clever process. Mr Sato barely had time to marvel at the machine before his noodles were done. He was so enamoured by the process that he even forgot to pause the machine and loosen the noodles while they were cooking, as recommended, but as these were instant noodles, which are hard to stuff up, he figured no harm was done. ▼ Another misstep was adding green onions as a topping for 100 yen, because the ramen already contained freeze-dried green onions in the packet. As a lover of green onions, Mr Sato didn’t mind having extra, and when he took a slurp he was pleased to find that the noodles were pleasantly chewy, with a lovely texture . The beef bone broth had plenty of flavour and a satisfying depth of umami, giving the dish a distinctly Korean taste. The noodles were hot and hearty, and Mr Sato particularly loved slurping them up inside the store, as it reminded him of the old “ auto parlors ” that used to exist along national highways in Japan in the ‘70s. These 24-hour rest stops were filled with arcade games and vending machines that served drinks and hot meals like ramen, making them particularly popular with long-haul truck drivers. Mr Sato would also stop by to use them in his hometown of Shimane when he owned a car and had late-night cravings for noodles. He recalled one particularly cold winter, when he’d woken up in the middle of the night and couldn’t get back to sleep, so he drove over to the auto parlor and had himself a bowl of noodles. The store was completely deserted, with nothing but the background noise of the arcade games keeping him company as he slurped away. It was lonely, but somehow comforting and warm, and he remembered how those noodles tasted so good. Looking back, that was a real moment of luxury, and it was one he thought he would never experience ever again. Though it wasn’t exactly the same, eating ramen at Noodle’s 24 brought him right back to that night with its auto parlor vibes. As a little hideaway where you can escape the hustle and bustle of the surrounding streets, this noodle joint is like an auto parlor right in the heart of Harajuku, and as they’re now pretty much non-existent in the way they used to be, any place that recreates the feel of an auto parlor is a great place to be. title: Wild Pikachu tree appears in Japan! [Video]
summary: Niigata town suddenly realizes part of its forests can do super-effective Pokémon cosplay. You don’t have to be a catch-‘em-all completionist to see the appeal of the setting of the Pokémon games and anime. The idea that you could head out into the countryside and suddenly encounter something as cute and cool as a wild […]
details: Niigata town suddenly realizes part of its forests can do super-effective Pokémon cosplay . You don’t have to be a catch-‘em-all completionist to see the appeal of the setting of the Pokémon games and anime. The idea that you could head out into the countryside and suddenly encounter something as cute and cool as a wild Pikachu is enough to get anyone excited. Of course, such whimsical adventures don’t happen in the real world, right? Well, maybe they do, if you happen to be in Niigata Prefecture right now, where this recently appeared. In a sleepy part of the town of Nagaoka , just a little off Niigata Prefectural Road 171 and a bit west of the Shibumigawa River, there’s a gingko tree that looks almost exactly like Pikachu . Though the tree itself isn’t new, it wasn’t until a few days ago that it started getting attention, as its leaves, now in their bright-yellow fall color, make the resemblance to the Pokémon mascot especially striking. As the only gingko tree in that part of the foothills, the silhouette really stands out, and if you’re fan of the franchise, it’s hard to see it as anything other than Pikachu. Reactions from online commenters have included: “It’s a wild Pikachu!” “This isn’t even like ‘Yeah, now that you mention it…’ That’s totally Pikachu.” “No way to not see that as Pikachu.” “Do gingko trees dream of electric mice?” “No throwing Poké Balls at the tree, everybody.” “I feel like if this had happened 200 years ago, people would have said ‘There’s a demon in the tree’ or ‘This is an evil omen.’ I’m glad to be living in the present day.” “Does this mean we’re going to see Pikachu here in the fall next year too?” “I hope it evolves into Raichu.” Unlike with Japan’s rice paddy art , this doesn’t appear to have been a planned, man-made art project. At the very least, no one’s come forward claiming to have been behind it, so for now it appears to simply be a genuinely cool coincidence. This sort of diagonally split top is an unusual feature for a gingko tree, but Google Streetview shows that the tree has been in that shape since at least August of this year, when the leaves were still green and no one had realized it was getting ready to cosplay as Pikachu. If you do decide to head to this part of Nagaoka to check out Mother Nature’s Pokémon fan art project, though, remember that this is a residential neighborhood, so make sure to be respectful to the locals, stay off of private property, and not leave any trash behind. And if you’re looking for even more Pokémon in Niigata, they’ve got some special Magikarp too . title: Taunting police by shouting “Shaolin Temple!” a growing trend among Japanese youth
summary: Patience, grasshoppers. I long ago have come to accept that part of getting old means not understanding what the kids are into these days. I like to think I’m still hip by appreciating the whimsical chaos of something like Italian brain rot, but with each passing day, young people seem to find new ways to […]
details: Patience, grasshoppers . I long ago have come to accept that part of getting old means not understanding what the kids are into these days. I like to think I’m still hip by appreciating the whimsical chaos of something like Italian brain rot, but with each passing day, young people seem to find new ways to baffle me. And I think today is the day I should finally start wearing suspenders and taking a vested interest in my digestion, because I have no idea what these kids are into. It’s being called the Shaolin Temple (“ Shorinji ” in Japanese) craze, and despite its name, it has seemingly nothing to do with warrior monks, Kung Fu , Wu Tang Clan, or the Japanese martial art Shorinji Kempo. The core concept of Shaolin Temple, also known as Shaolin Temple Racing, is annoying police officers. In Japan, there are a network of police outposts called “ koban ” that serve as places you can go to turn in lost items, report crimes, or seek refuge if someone is after you. They’re often manned by around two officers at a time. These huts also serve as prime targets for Shaolin Temple kids. The standard prank is similar to ding-dong-ditch, in that the kids will open the door to the Koban, scream “Shaolin Temple!” and then run away giggling. Some even go as far as jumping on the koban’s counter or prank calling the emergency hotline, 110, to shout the name of a temple at them. In every case, the stunts, ranging from annoying to criminal, are recorded on video and shared on social media. ▼ A news report showing some clips of Shaolin Temple incidents According to reports, students from elementary school to high school have been detained or arrested for Shaolin Temple activities in the western prefectures of Osaka, Hyogo, Hiroshima, and Toyama, though it may only be a matter of time before the fad spreads further. ▼ Although not common in their area yet, a few days ago, the Tokyo Metropolitan Police took pre-emptive action and issued a warning that barging into a koban and shouting “Shaolin Temple” constitutes unlawful entry and is punishable by up to three years in a correctional facility or a 100,000 yen (US$630) fine. 【警視庁少年事件課からの重大なお知らせ】 「少林寺レーシング」と呼ばれる事案について 本当に警察を必要としている人の対処が遅れます。 悪ふざけでは済まされません。 警察は厳正に対処します。 pic.twitter.com/oo7iJVf82I — 警視庁生活安全部 (@MPD_yokushi) November 20, 2026 No one is really sure why the kids are shouting “Shaolin Temple” of all things. Even kids who got caught and questioned by police can’t explain it, though it seems very likely the charm lies in the absurdity of it all. Many comments online, however, saw very little charm in the acts themselves and felt that social media and kids don’t mix. “It’s the sense of unifying with peers and the thrill of doing something forbidden. Even if Shaolin Temple fades away, that spirit will remain.” “The police should post videos of the punishments that come about in the Shaolin Temple aftermaths. That might help curb this trend.” “Kids have been playing poli-oni [‘police onigoko’ or ‘police tag,’ hitting a police car to make it chase you] for over a decade now, but we can’t have police distracted when they’re needed for serious problems.” “It just goes to show that the way to get popular on social media is to cater to the mentality of a 10-year-old.” “They have no idea how lame that looks.” “We should follow Australia’s example and ban social media for kids.” “I’m feeling second-hand embarrassment just watching it.” “I won’t stand for them dragging Shaolin’s name through the mud.” It does seem like we’re due for another Kung Fu reboot, perhaps this time in the wild west of Japan. Shaolin monk Kwai Chang Caine narrowly escapes assassination in China and finds himself in Kansai , only to learn that his temple’s name is being used as a mere prank. He travels from town to town, teaching youngsters the true way of Shaolin and solving mysteries, with a guest appearance by William Shatner. As for reality, I just hope kids can come to their senses and have fun the way we did before social media, by wearing beards made of bees and putting ferrets down our pants. title: This bento boxed lunch we got at a Japanese supermarket felt like a scam, but maybe it’s not
summary: Can we find it in our hearts and stomachs to forgive this deceptive-looking bento? There’s a type of boxed lunch in Japan called the makunouchi bento, which is a boxed lunch with…well, pretty much whatever the person making it wants to put in there. Makunouchi doesn’t refer to any specific dish or ingredient. It actually […]
details: Can we find it in our hearts and stomachs to forgive this deceptive-looking bento? There’s a type of boxed lunch in Japan called the makunouchi bento , which is a boxed lunch with…well, pretty much whatever the person making it wants to put in there. Makunouchi doesn’t refer to any specific dish or ingredient. It actually just means, roughly, “behind the curtain,” and it originally referred to the boxed lunches eaten by theater workers during the Edo period, which consisted of white rice and whatever assorted small side dishes could be cooked or procured in and around the theater. Eventually, makunouchi bento became popular with audiences too, and then the general public, and now you can find them for sale even if you’re nowhere near the stage, including at just about any Japanese supermarket. Now, buying a boxed lunch with a name that basically just means “rice and stuff” might seem like a huge risk, but the way that bento contents are arranged makes it easy to see what kind of sides you’re getting just by looking at it. For example, the makunouchi bento our Japanese-language reporter Yayoi Saginomiya recently picked up at budget-friendly supermarket chain Seiyu had rice sprinkled with black sesame seeds, nikudango (meatballs), kinpira gobo (stewed burdock root and carrot), tamagoyaki (a Japanese-style omelet), half a potato croquette, and benishoga (pickled ginger) . Then, at the center of it all, was a slice of grilled salmon . The salmon is definitely meant to be the star of the show here. Not only does Seiyu label this boxed lunch as a Coho/Silver Salmon Makunouchi Bento , the lid has a sticker on it proudly boasting that the slice of fish is flame-grilled before going into the box. After arriving back home, Yayoi sat down, removed the lid, and got ready to dig in. Naturally, the first thing she wanted to try was that salmon, but as she angled her chopsticks toward it she couldn’t help noticing, now that she was looking looking at it from this perspective… …that it was really thin . And we mean really, really thin. It couldn’t have been more than 5 millimeters (0.2 inches) in thickness. It was so thin that even one of Yayoi’s chopsticks, at the thicker end, had more girth. At this point, Yayoi couldn’t help feeling ripped off, and we were having flashbacks to the convenience store “paper tiger sandwich” scandal that hit a while back. Granted, at 538 yen (US$3.40) this is a pretty inexpensive bento by today’s market conditions, but still, that’s a laughably thin cut of fish, and Yayoi can’t ever remember seeing grilled salmon sliced this thin before. OK, so this bento is pitifully lacking in its quantity of salmon, but what about its quality? Actually, Yayoi has got no complaints at all on that front. Compared to other types of salmon, coho salmon tends to have more fat, making it moist and tender. Those qualities were definitely present here, and the extent to which the fish had been grilled was pretty much perfect . All of the other side dishes were excellent as well . The meatballs had just the right texture, neither tough nor mushy. The kinpira gobo was expertly seasoned, with the sweet, soy sauce notes of its broth pleasing the palate, as did the stimulatingly sweet tamagoyaki. The croquette had gotten a little limp as it had cooled off, but its flavor hadn’t suffered at all, and even the ginger worked great as a little sharp accent. Again, there’s no getting around how thin and meager the cut of salmon is. After eating it, though, Yayoi came to the conclusion that, with costs going up, if a bento maker is going to try to keep their prices the same, she’d rather they keep the quality high, even if that means smaller portions, as opposed to maintaining the same size of all the dishes by switching to cheaper, poorer-tasting ingredients . Still, Seiyu could stand to be a little more upfront about this, and odds are they’re not the only ones putting their bento components in the box in ways that make it hard to gauge their full size, so we’d recommend taking a close look from various angles if you really want to be sure of how big a lunch your boxed lunch is going to be. details: Trending GTA 6 Modern Warfare 4 Twitch EA FC 27 Wardogs Entertainment Anime Clannad and Angel Beats creator opts against active cancer treatment to focus on work by James Busby Published: Oct 19, 2026, 12:59 Save for later Save for later VisualArts/Key Add as a preferred source on Google Follow on Google News The creator behind Clannad and the anime series Angel Beats has been diagnosed with throat cancer and has chosen to focus on palliative care so he can continue creating. On October 19, Visual Arts, the company Maeda works for, confirmed that he is currently hospitalized after being diagnosed with throat cancer. After considering his condition and the outlook for treatment, Maeda has decided against active treatment to conserve his strength for his creative work. The company also shared an update on his contributions to Heaven Burns Red and a new music project, which he now hopes to complete more quickly following his diagnosis. Article continues after ad Clannad writer shares health update and plans for future projects In its official statement, Visual Arts said Maeda began experiencing throat discomfort in early spring. However, a subsequent medical examination found that the swelling and pain became more pronounced over the summer. “After careful consideration of his condition and the outlook for treatment, Maeda has chosen not to pursue active treatment and instead to focus on palliative care, wishing to conserve his strength and devote himself to his creative work,” the company said. Article continues after ad Maeda has already completed his assigned writing for Heaven Burns Red’s main story through the first half of Chapter 6. He has also finished all the major story elements that will carry the narrative through the chapter’s conclusion, along with the lyrics and composition for songs featured in its first half. Article continues after ad However, Visual Arts said the progression of his illness could prevent him from participating in the creation of other scenarios and songs. Amazon Maeda also worked on Angel Beats as a planner and writer, and composed the anime’s music. Alongside his work on the game, Maeda had been developing an original music project with plans to release new songs on YouTube over the long term. His diagnosis has prompted him to change that approach. “He felt that there was little time remaining in which he would be able to continue creating,” the statement said. At his request, the finished works will be released on YouTube. Article continues after ad “Maeda is currently hospitalized, but even under these circumstances, he remains strongly determined to devote himself to creative work through to the very end,” the company said. “We would be grateful for your warm understanding and support of his wishes.” Fans wishing to send messages of encouragement can do so by using the email address at the bottom of the English statement . title: Student sparks police investigation after bringing ‘Death Note’ book to school
summary: A Massachusetts student’s ‘Death Note’ notebook prompted a suspension and a real police investigation, with one parent demanding stronger action.
details: Trending GTA 6 Modern Warfare 4 Twitch EA FC 27 Wardogs Entertainment Student sparks police investigation after bringing ‘Death Note’ book to school by Michael Gwilliam Published: Oct 12, 2026, 14:51 Save for later Save for later Netflix Add as a preferred source on Google Follow on Google News A Massachusetts student’s ‘Death Note’ notebook prompted a suspension and a real police investigation, with one parent demanding stronger action despite officials finding no immediate threat. In Death Note , Light Yagami’s notebook attracts the attention of a mysterious detective known as L. At Chocksett Middle School in Sterling, a student’s version brought in local police. Administrators contacted officers on September 30 after discovering the notebook. Students had already been dismissed when police responded. Article continues after ad The student explained to staff it was connected to the manga and anime, in which Light uses a supernatural notebook to kill criminals by writing their names inside. Student suspended after Death Note concerns According to Boston.com , principal Tina Boss said investigators interviewed dozens of students and found no evidence the notebook was intended to threaten the school or any particular student. “Based on the information gathered, including dozens of student interviews and the investigation conducted by the Sterling Police Department, our multidisciplinary team has found no indication that the notebook or its contents were intended as a threat toward the school or any particular student,” she told the community. Article continues after ad Article continues after ad “The information indicates that the notebook was indeed connected to a television series and an inappropriate theme that has made its way into the school,” she added, further saying the book was from an anime with an “inappropriate theme.” Madhouse Police found no immediate threat and said they were not seeking criminal charges based on the available information. However, the explanation that it was inspired by Light’s fictional notebook did little to reassure parent Jen DiCandia. She said her daughter’s name appeared inside and challenged the student’s return following a three-day suspension. Related Teachers panic after finding student’s ‘Death Note’ at LeBron James’ I Promise school School suspends autistic 6-year-old for biting sandwich into shape of gun Death Note fans still wish one thing was different about the ending Article continues after ad “She deserves to feel safe in her classroom, every single day,” DiCandia wrote. The family has since retained an attorney, Sentinel & Enterprise reported . DiCandia said the students still shared three classes and called for them to be permanently separated at school. “My goal is for my daughter to attend school safely and continue her education without fear,” she said. “I don’t really care if it’s a joke, a video game, whatever. It’s not funny.” Article continues after ad Article continues after ad Death Note notebooks have a long history of causing trouble at school Ryuk’s notebook has inspired plenty of real-world imitations, and Sterling is far from the first school to investigate one. In September 2026, a 12-year-old in Florida was arrested after a ‘Death Note’ listing students and staff was found at Argyle Elementary School . title: Japan celebrates anime couple getting together after 28 years with trucks and a boat
summary: Two anime characters have finally become a couple after 28 years of “will they/won’t they” moments, and Japan is celebrating their long-awaited relationship with advertising trucks and a boat showcasing their romance.
details: Trending GTA 6 Modern Warfare 4 Twitch EA FC 27 Wardogs TV & Movies Anime Japan celebrates anime couple getting together after 28 years with trucks and a boat by James Busby Published: Oct 12, 2026, 13:18 Save for later Save for later TMS Entertainment Add as a preferred source on Google Follow on Google News Two anime characters have finally become a couple after 28 years of “will they/won’t they” moments, and Japan is celebrating their long-awaited relationship with advertising trucks and a boat showcasing their romance. Slow-burning relationships are nothing new for anime fans, just look at the likes of Naruto and Hinata. However, fans rarely have to wait nearly three decades for characters who clearly love one another to become Facebook official. For fans of Detective Conan, that’s exactly what has happened as one of the show’s longest-running romances has finally taken a major step forward. On October 10, Heiji Hattori and Kazuha Toyama officially became a couple after 28 long years of waiting. Article continues after ad The couple getting together has proven so huge that trucks and a boat are now touring around Japan’s streets with artwork celebrating their relationship. 大阪歩いてたらすごい車走ってたwwww #名探偵コナン #茜色の千秋楽 #浪速のビッグカップル pic.twitter.com/UTihI0ezvX — こなぴくん🪶興行収入実況 (@CNP___boxoffice) October 11, 2026 Detective Conan characters finally become a couple Osaka high school detective Heiji Hattori and his childhood friend Kazuha Toyama have spent decades dancing around their feelings for each other. In fact, Kazuha first appeared in the anime in 1998, and ever since then, the pair have left viewers patiently waiting for their romance to blossom. Article continues after ad If you’ve seen any anime, chances are you’ve seen how painful it can be for characters to get to a stage where they can even hold hands or go in for that big first kiss. Combine this with the fact that it’s taken 28 years to reach this moment, and you have something that is on par with Ross and Rachel’s relationship from Friends, but just with even more waiting. Article continues after ad According to a translated report via Livedoor News , advertising trucks celebrating the pair are currently traveling through Osaka’s Umeda, Shinsaibashi, and Namba areas until October 17. Meanwhile, a boat carrying ads celebrating the couple will be cruising along the Dotonbori River from 4 pm each day until October 13. ╭━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╮ 祝！平次♡和葉 #茜色の千秋楽 お祝いアドクルーズ運航中⛴️ ╰━ｖ━━━━━━━━━━━━╯ 10/11(日)～10/13(火)まで 夕方4時から道頓堀川を運航中 あの戎橋も通ります🎉 「茜色の千秋楽（大楽）」は TVerで見逃し配信中🎬 pic.twitter.com/PijP1KXVo0 — アニメ名探偵コナン【公式】⚽️ (@conan_anime1000) October 11, 2026 While Detective Conan fans have been rejoicing over the long-awaited romance, Heiji’s voice actor, Ryo Horikawa, also reflected on how the confession finally unfolded after years of failed attempts. Article continues after ad Related Hatsune Miku takes over Tokyo Metro with themed train and hotel room Hatsune Miku’s husband wants more anime fans to marry their favorite characters Jujutsu Kaisen is reuniting Gojo and Geto soon, and fans can’t keep calm Article continues after ad “At first, I imagined all sorts of ways he might confess. I wondered whether he would look Kazuha straight in the eyes and tell her he loved her,” he said. “But after so many failed attempts, his feelings just slipped out, and Kazuha happened to overhear him. It became something like, ‘Is that really true?’ followed by, ‘It’s true!’” Horikawa also had a message for his character: “Heiji Hattori, you lucky guy! Take good care of Kazuha. Oh, and Ryo Horikawa is rooting for the two of them too. After all, I’m Heiji.” Article continues after ad コナンのテーマソング聞こえると思ったら さすが大阪だ pic.twitter.com/Nb15nSzsYN — みく (@yummy102) October 11, 2026 Kazuha’s voice actor, Yuko Miyamura, was equally pleased to see the two characters finally become a couple. “Finally!! Heiji’s confession was a success, and their feelings for each other have finally been confirmed!” she said. “Everyone around them already knew they liked each other, but he had to go looking for a spectacular spot to rival Big Ben. Honestly, it took so long!” Article continues after ad Despite the decades that have passed for viewers, Miyamura noted that considerably less time has elapsed within the story. Article continues after ad Detective Conan fans in Japan can also relive the confession at Osaka’s Abeno Harukas, the real building that inspired its setting. Starting October 11, the Harukas 300 observation deck features footprints marking where the characters stood, alongside audio from the anime. An exclusive conversation never shown in the anime or manga will play in the elevator on the way down, which will reveal what Heiji and Kazuha said after the confession. It’s all rather wholesome stuff. Now we just need to see what stunts Japan will pull when protagonist Shinichi Kudo finally ties the knot with Ran Mori. Maybe a national holiday? title: After years of catering to foreign tourists, Osaka’s Kuromon Market wants locals to come back
summary: It’s been a long time since many Osaka residents did their shopping in “Osaka’s kitchen.” Kuromon Market, or Kuromon Ichiba in Japanese, is a collection of roughly 150 shops along a 600-meter (1,969-foot) covered shopping arcade in Osaka’s Minami neighborhood. details: It’s been a long time since many Osaka residents did their shopping in “Osaka’s kitchen.” Kuromon Market , or Kuromon Ichiba in Japanese, is a collection of roughly 150 shops along a 600-meter (1,969-foot) covered shopping arcade in Osaka’s Minami neighborhood. The market traces its history back to some 200 years ago, having started in the Edo period, and it’s sometimes been referred to as “Osaka’s kitchen.” That nickname isn’t particularly accurate anymore, as in recent years Kuromon’s shops have shifted heavily towards catering to foreign travelers looking for photogenic street food instead of Osaka residents shopping for groceries. Now, though, Kuromon is looking to win back locals’ favor as tourist numbers start to dip. Kuromon started out as a place where locals would buy basics such as fish, vegetables, tofu, and mochi. As time went on, some shops evolved into a sort of hybrid operation that sold both ingredients and prepared foods, and as more tourists started coming to the market for sightseeing, those prepared foods started shifting from everyday staples to more luxurious, flashy-looking, or simply inflated-price street foods, prices that local shoppers would balk at, but that travelers, who’d come to the market for special-occasion entertainment rather than errands, could more happily swallow. This trend accelerated as overseas travelers started to outnumber locals at the market by a wide margin. With foreign tourists’ wallets stuffed with cash thanks to the weak yen, many of Kuromon’s merchants went all in on appealing to them, further pricing out locals to the point where many of them now see the market first and foremost as a tourist attraction/trap. ▼ Even the discounted 5,800 yen (US$36.50) is a ridiculous price for such a small tempura assortment, especially if you’re eating it in a casual market and not a fancy restaurant. 錦市場の次は、大阪の黒門市場にも来ていただきたいコケ https://t.co/SzOd6oSVvr pic.twitter.com/8PZjuTej3I — ぽんタブ │ NIPPON-BASHI SHOP HEADLINE │ 大阪・日本橋 (@dendentown) November 7, 2026 The problem for Kuromon, though, is that Osaka isn’t attracting quite as many tourists these days . Though overall inbound tourist traffic to Japan remains high, there’s been a significant dip in the number of visitors from China, a demographic that’s traditionally made up an especially big proportion of Osaka’s foreign tourism. So with Kuromon seeing fewer foreign tourist customers these days, the market is now trying to woo back locals . The efforts to do so are a joint project between the Kuromon Market Promotional Association, Osaka Metropolitan University, Kyoto Iken (a medical and health care specialty school), and the Kinki Newspaper Insert Advertising Association. Part of the plan involves leveraging students’ social media savvy, having teams of the teens and 20-somethings find shops and products in the market and showcasing them in posts to introduce “the Kuromon Market that Osaka residents don’t know about,” and the market started its own official Instagram account this past October . ▼ Kuromon Market’s official mascot character, Mon-chan, is an anthropomorphic kuromon (black gate). View this post on Instagram On the other end of the technological spectrum, Kuromon Market also recently printed 60,000 insert advertisements to be tucked into local newspapers. The market is also holding its first-ever Black Friday sale this year, running from November 18 to 28 (Japanese businesses have basically adapted Black Friday to just indicate “November sale”). However, convincing locals to come back to the market is something that’s easier said than done . While some not unanimously negative, online reactions to some of Kuromon’s attempts show that there’s still some resentment towards the market for the foreign-tourist focus it’s had for the past several years. “What, they’re going to have students tell each other to come drop 5,000-yen (US$31) for a basic lunch?” “What a joke. Their food is way too expensive for Japanese locals. Good luck with selling it to foreign tourists.” “That’s what you get for throwing away your local customers and just trying to profit off inbound tourists.” “A while back, I was curious to see how badly Kuromon Market rips people off, so I went to take a look around…The prices were so ridiculous that it was actually kind of entertaining to see them, but I didn’t buy anything.” “I remember them complaining about not having enough customers during the pandemic and pleading for locals to come…Then when the pandemic ended [and tourism opened up again] the prices went right back up.” “They got themselves into this mess. Let them cry about it all they want.” “They really gotta stop that habit of trying to cozy up to locals to help them out as soon as things start to go bad.” Again, that’s not to say that everyone has written off Kuromon for good, and a number of online reactions to posts about the Black Friday sale have been from Japanese people saying they’re interested in paying the place a visit for the first time in a while. Still, there are clearly a lot of people whose image of the market has changed enough that they’ve lost all interest in it. It’s worth keeping in mind that, for the entity of the two centuries that Kuromon Market has been around, its shops have always been businesses, and adapting to current economic conditions has long been one of the best ways for businesses to financially succeed. As Kuromon started getting more foreign tourists with more money to spend and an appetite for premium-priced products, it’s understandable that shops would want to give them what they want and make bigger profits for themselves. This eventually became a sort of self-propelling cycle: as more shops started offering more expensive foods, that in turn drew more tourists, so even fewer locals came to the market, so the focus on catering to tourists got even stronger. title: 100-meter (328-foot) tall Dragon Quest Slime, Final Fantasy Chocobo art to appear in Yokohama
summary: It’s time for the mascots of Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest to make their Cosmo Clock debuts. The city of Yokohama is hosting some very special guests this holiday season. As part of a collaboration with Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest, Chocobo and Slime, the video game franchises’ respective mascot monsters, are hanging out in […]
details: It’s time for the mascots of Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest to make their Cosmo Clock debuts . The city of Yokohama is hosting some very special guests this holiday season. As part of a collaboration with Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest , Chocobo and Slime , the video game franchises’ respective mascot monsters, are hanging out in the Minato Mirai harbor district, where special FF and DQ Christmas trees have gone up, and where fans can grab a bite to eat at a limited-time themed cafe . The decorations include some huge Slime and Chocobo balloons, but the two stars are now getting even bigger. When you have a guest, it’s only appropriate that you give them the nicest seat in the house, and Minato Mirai does something similar for visiting characters by giving them a spot on the Cosmo Clock , the neighborhood’s massive, 100-meter (328-foot) diameter Ferris wheel . They did it for Hello Kitty , Pikachu , and Evangelion Unit-01 , and now they’re doing it for Slime and Chocobo! ーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーー #DQFF横浜みなとみらい 最新情報 ーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーーー 大観覧車「コスモクロック21」が、DQ・FF仕様の特別演出に 期間限定の仕様をお見逃しなく https://t.co/6Ly5IDGSpR 11月21日（土）～29日（日） pic.twitter.com/fezQYDX7B2 — ドラゴンクエスト宣伝担当 (@DQ_PR) November 18, 2026 From November 21 to 29 , the two characters will be appearing in the illuminated spokes of the Ferris wheel (there are 60 of them, and the tips light up sequentially at a rate of one per second, hence the “Cosmo Clock” name). Minato Mirai is already famous for its nighttime views, but Slime and Chocobo are sure to draw even more fans, and to help them plan their visit the pair will be appearing at a set schedule nightly between 6:30 and 8:45 p.m., at the top of plus 15, 30, and 45 minutes of each hour . ▼ Preview images give a sense of the gigantic scale. The Cosmo Clock, officially known as Cosmo Clock 21, is located inside the Cosmo World amusement park, just a short walk from the Landmark Plaza and Mark Is shopping centers with the Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest Christmas decorations. Because of how big the Ferris wheel is, though, you don’t necessarily need to be on the park grounds to see it, and even if you want to take a look close up, Cosmo World doesn’t charge admission, as visitors instead pay for tickets for specific rides. Unfortunately, the schedule means that fans will have to hurry to see the giant Cosmo Clock Slime and Chocobo for themselves, but don’t worry, the rest of their Christmas decorations will be up through the start of next year. title: Tomb festival in Osaka holds qualifying tyrannosaurus race and ancient clay sculpture chase
summary: Ready to unpack all that? Monday 23 November is a public holiday in Japan, creating a long weekend this year, which is always a good time to hold a major event. In Osaka, that meant it was time once again for Kofun Fest Hanicotto, a regional festival celebrating ancient Japanese graves at Imajozuka Kofun Park. […]
details: Ready to unpack all that? Monday 23 November is a public holiday in Japan, creating a long weekend this year, which is always a good time to hold a major event. In Osaka, that meant it was time once again for Kofun Fest Hanicotto, a regional festival celebrating ancient Japanese graves at Imajozuka Kofun Park . A kofun is an ancient tomb typically reserved for royalty. Since Osaka was an ancient capital of Japan and adjacent to other historical capitals like Nara and Kyoto, the city is dotted with quite a few of them, easily spotted in aerial photos due to their large sizes and distinctive, keyhole-like shapes. ▼ Here are a few of them. As for “Hanicotto,” that is a combination of the words “ haniwa ” and the Japanese pronunciation of “mascot.” Players of Animal Crossing ought to be somewhat familiar with the ancient clay sculptures known as haniwa that resemble scared or confused cactuses. These figures were buried with the deceased in kofun to help protect them in the afterlife. ▼ Kofun Fest Hanicotto was also the venue for HaniCon 2026. With all this talk of fifth-century Japanese culture, you’re probably wondering, “This is all well and good, but why aren’t there any dinosaurs here, too?” Well, I was just getting to that. For a few years now, Kofun Fest Hanicotto has also been the host of the West Japan qualifying round of the Tyranno Fest national Tyrannosaurus rex race . This is the only qualifying race of its kind on this side of Japan and promises to bring the very best in men, women, and children who run around while wearing a big T-Rex costume. The first and second-place male and female racers, as well as one wildcard entrant who wins the MIP (Most Impressive Participant) award, advance to Tyranno Fest Vol. 3 on 20 March, 2027 at Funabashi Racecourse in Chiba Prefecture . The Kofun Fest Hanicotto races are prestigious events in this dignified spot. At Tyranno Fest Vol. 1, the women’s champion came from Kofun Fest Hanicotto, as did the men’s champ in Tyranno Fest Vol. 2. This grand prix of T-Rex racing is a gate-style sprint, in which the dinos start behind closed gates like racehorses, presumably because it looks really funny. These qualifying rounds, however, are standard time trial races, combined with Kofun Fest Hanicotto’s signature Haniwa Capture Race , where the Tyrannosaurus Rexes have to also pick up haniwa statues on the ground, and probably fall down a lot in the process. The main sponsor of this event is none other than Zenpo-Koenfu , a grave operator that has made headlines for their award-winning modern Takeda-style kofun tombs . The centerpiece of these is a stylish reimagining of the ancient burial grounds that lies atop Mt. Ikoma, overlooking nearly all of Osaka Prefecture in a picturesque park designed by the firm of noted architect Tadao Ando. It won the Kansai Region Grave Grand Prix for both its layout and as a convenient, cost-effective alternative to traditional family graves. All in all, it’s a great time to learn about Japanese burial methods old and new, while also watching people dressed as dinosaurs wobble around for a bit . Although this year’s event is behind us now, it’s sure to return next year, bigger and more ancient than ever. title: Conveyor belt sushi chain Sushiro quadruples its prices for first branch in America
summary: Enthusiastic diners show up for Sushiro’s opening in New York, fans in Japan experience sushi sticker shock. Last week, Japanese conveyor belt sushi chain Sushiro made its American debut. The chain’s first-ever branch on U.S. soil, located in New York, welcomed its first customers on November 19 with long lines of diners waiting to get […]
details: Enthusiastic diners show up for Sushiro’s opening in New York, fans in Japan experience sushi sticker shock . Last week, Japanese conveyor belt sushi chain Sushiro made its American debut. The chain’s first-ever branch on U.S. soil, located in New York , welcomed its first customers on November 19 with long lines of diners waiting to get in. It’s not just Manhattanites’ whose attention has been grabbed, though, as people in Sushiro’s home country of Japan have been shocked at the prices being charged by the New York branch . As you can see in the above video, Sushiro wasn’t hurting for customers on its opening day, with some people arriving hours before its 11 a.m. opening in order to be some of the first seated. Diners seemed very happy with the quality of the food too in the on-site interviews that have been posted. Sushiro has brought over several aspects of the chain’s dining experience from Japan, including large tough-screen panels for placing orders and a no-tipping policy , which is the norm in Japan but a rarity for restaurants in America. That doesn’t meant that Sushiro is positioning itself as a budget restaurant in the States, though, as its prices start from US$5 a plate for standard types of sushi like maguro (tuna), and more expensive ingredients, like otoro (extra-fatty tuna) cost US$10. Those prices convert to about 800 and 1,600 yen. Meanwhile, if you go to a Sushiro in Japan… …you can get a plate of maguro for 180 yen, and the vast majority of its sushi can be had for 210 yen or les s . In other words, Sushiro is charging about four times as much in the U.S. as it does in Japan . Is that too much? That’s actually a pretty complicated question. Right off the bat, the yen is extremely weak versus the U.S. dollar right now, so it’s natural for prices to be higher in the U.S. In addition, Sushiro’s first American branch is in Manhattan, one of the most expensive neighborhoods in one of the most expensive cities in the country. If we figure an average-sized sushi meal is going to be somewhere within the range of 5 to 10 plates, that’s make a meal at Sushiro New York cost US$25-US$50. That’s not an eye-popping price for a meal out in Americas these days, and even if we convert that to 4,000-8,000 yen, that’s not a shocking amount of money for one person to spend on a restaurant sushi meal in Japan. It is, however, a startling amount of money for someone in Japan to spend on a Sushiro meal. In the Japanese restaurant industry, you could say that Sushiro occupies a space similar to the one In-N-Out Burger has in America . For its segment and price point, it has a reputation for excellent quality, and so it has a lot of loyal fans, enough that you’ll often find long lines during the lunch or dinner rush, or when a new branch opens and marks the chain’s first arrival in a neighborhood. However, no one in Japan considers Sushiro to be high-end dining. Sure, the food is tasty, but the décor, ambiance, and overall vibe isn’t particularly luxurious or otherwise rarified, so quadrupling the price really messes with its perception as being good quality at a good price, leading to online reactions in Japan about the New York opening such as: “800 yen a plate? Man, America is expensive…” “Way too steep, No way I’m eating Sushiro at that price!” “I can’t even laugh at how expensive that is.” “It’s nice that they say ‘no tips,’ but it’s crazy to [quadruple] the price compared to Japan.” “I can get a whole lunch for 800 yen.” “People are seriously lining up down the street and paying those prices to ear at a basic chain restaurant?” “I don’t think it’s gonna last.” Ultimately, though, all that really matters is whether diners in New York are OK with those prices, and that’s something we won’t know for a while . Again, figuring a price of US$25-$US$40 for a meal, Sushiro isn’t an exorbitantly expensive option by American restaurant prices, but it’s also not a particularly cheap one either, especially for customers with big appetites who’ll need more than 10 plates to feel full. Because of that, Sushiro really is going to have to convince customers that it’s a restaurant worth paying a bit of a price premium for, and to that end, the interior does look a little fancier than what you’d see at a Sushiro branch. The New York branch also has private rooms for groups of diners, though these also are for more expensive fixed-price course meals. ▼ One of the Sushiro New York private dining rooms can be seen in the video here. On the other hand, there’s a risk that the conveyor belt delivery system and giant touch panel used for ordering, once the novelty wears off, might seem more gimmicky than high-tech classy, and no matter how nice the restaurant’s interior is, being located right next door to a McDonald’s could also impact how special a visit to Sushiro feels, at least in terms of being someplace at which to splurge on an expensive, or at least not-cheap, meal. For now, though, it looks like Sushiro is off to a good start in the States, and can now focus on finding ways to keep customers coming back. title: New Fuji Tram system is in development to help curb crowds, lessen environmental impact of cars
summary: The tram route will connect the base of Mt. Fuji with the Yoshida Trail’s 5th Station as well as the under-construction Chuo Shinkansen maglev line. Yamanashi Prefecture unveiled plans on November 18 for a new public transportation system dubbed the Fuji Tram, with its name confirmed to be changed in the future. The tram will […]
details: The tram route will connect the base of Mt. Fuji with the Yoshida Trail’s 5th Station as well as the under-construction Chuo Shinkansen maglev line . Yamanashi Prefecture unveiled plans on November 18 for a new public transportation system dubbed the Fuji Tram , with its name confirmed to be changed in the future. The tram will take over the Fujikyu bus route currently in place along the Fuji Subaru Line toll road from the base of Mt. Fuji, where a new station is to be built (most likely on the west side of the Fujisan Parking lot) to the Yoshida Trail 5th Station, which is the most popular starting place for climbers. After the tram begins operations, private vehicles, buses, and taxis will no longer be allowed to use the road per Japan’s Road Traffic Act. ▼ This promotional video for the Fuji Tram also details plans to connect its new station with other regional tourism hotspots, including the Linear Chuo Shinkansen maglev line that’s currently under construction. The adoption of the tram system is not meant to curb anyone’s fun but is a measure aimed at controlling the number of visitors and reducing the environmental impact of vehicles on Japan’s highest mountain . Yamanashi Prefecture previously imposed new daily climber restrictions and fees that went into effect last year, but concerns of overtourism still remain. The Fuji Tram plans are slated to restrict the number of visitors to the 5th Station to 2.3 million people annually , which is roughly on par with the number of visitors in 2012 before Mt. Fuji became a UNESCO World Heritage Site the following year. When selecting this limit, the government also took measures to avoid having the drop in visitors result in a negative impact on local economies. Regarding the tram’s production, three different environmentally conscious plans are currently being considered: a Chinese-manufactured hydrogen and electric vehicle , as well as two different European-manufactured electric vehicles. All plans involve a vehicle with linked cars and rubber tires, though the former would be able to run in two directions while the latter only in a single direction. Total estimates for the construction and implementation costs are 77.3 billion to 96.5 billion yen (US$486.6 million to $607.5 million) depending on which plan is adopted, with the European electric vehicles costing on the lower end and the Chinese hydrogen and electric vehicle on the higher end. The project as a whole is expected to be funded by the third sector or Private a Finance Initiative (PFI) model. ▼ Capacity is expected to be 120 people per vehicle. While there’s no current estimate for the start of operations, the Fuji Tram is expected to take 52-67 minutes from the new base station to the 5th Station, with vehicles running every 6-15 minutes (7-8 minutes on average). Round-trip passenger fare will be within 10,000 yen per person. With the number of off-season climbers on Mt. Fuji facing increased scrutiny in Japan, hopefully the new Fuji Tram system will provide a more convenient and eco-friendly way for visitors to access the hiking trails during the mountain’s official climbing season as well. title: Open just three hours a day, a new Tokyo soba joint serves up wildly addictive regional noodles
summary: No need to travel up north for these thick, chewy noodles, but you’ll have to adapt your lunch schedule to match theirs. With ramen chains like Ichiran taking up a lot of social media screen time, it’s no wonder that ramen is one of Japan’s must-eat foods, but other noodle dishes throughout Japan hold just […]
details: No need to travel up north for these thick, chewy noodles, but you’ll have to adapt your lunch schedule to match theirs. With ramen chains like Ichiran taking up a lot of social media screen time, it’s no wonder that ramen is one of Japan’s must-eat foods, but other noodle dishes throughout Japan hold just as much importance in the country’s culinary scene, perhaps even more given their longer history, impact on culture, and more refined appeal. Buckwheat noodles , known as soba , are one such dish, having hundreds of years to work into the hearts and stomachs of Japan’s populace, culminating in several regional variations that are all equally a delight to enjoy. Our Japanese-language reporter P.K. Sanjun recently had his first experience with Yamagata soba , and was instantly addicted. The dark-colored, thick soba was extraordinarily filling and hearty, making for an insanely delicious bowl. However, he must admit that he needs to apologize to any geographic loyalists out there, as his first ever Yamagata soba was actually eaten in Sendai, Miyagi (its neighboring prefecture). As he thought back on that bowl of heaven, P.K. couldn’t help but wonder if it were possible to eat Yamagata soba in Tokyo too, and after doing some research, he discovered that the very shop he ate at in Sendai had opened its first Tokyo branch this year. Truly, this must be the work of the noodle gods calling him forth to fulfil his destiny. The name of the shop P.K. ate at in Sendai was Nikusoba Toshichi , and just as it suggests, the specialty of the shop is ‘nikusoba’ (literally ‘meat soba’). The meat in question is chicken, but more specifically chickens that have finished laying eggs, which are known as oyadori and have a deep umami and firm texture, and the broth is also apparently made from chicken. ▼ Nikusoba Toshichi’s Sendai branch However, P.K. had a lingering regret: the original specialty of the store is cold nikusoba , but Sendai on that day was terrifyingly cold, so the staff recommended the warm nikusoba instead. ▼ Warm nikusoba It was tremendously delicious, but he just couldn’t get over his desire to try it cold, so with the arrival of Nikusoba Toshichi’s expansion into central Tokyo, his chance for a redo arrived a lot sooner than he had anticipated. Located roughly between the Tokyo Metro’s Hanzomon and Nagatacho Subway Stations , a stone’s throw from the Imperial Palace, the new store was very conveniently situated. Business hours are the same three hours as in Sendai, 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m., and since it’s closed on Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays, your only option is to go on a weekday —which seems to be a power play by the store that says, “adjust your life to our noodle schedule, not the other way around.” Even so… Nikusoba Toshichi is worth it a hundred times over. After walking about five minutes from Hanzomon Station, P.K. arrived at the Hanzomon Branch and was greeted by a line of about ten people that had formed in front of the shop. Just like in the Sendai store, there was plenty of standing-room eating space, so the turnover is a lot faster than might be expected, meaning that P.K. only had about 15 minutes to wait before his turn arrived. P.K. ordered the Nikusoba Large Serving (1,050 yen [US$6.57], and topped it with gesoten (deep-fried squid tentacle tempura, a beloved regional pairing in Yamagata) for an additional 250 yen. What he hadn’t realized was that the large serving has an incredible 600 grams (about 1.3 pounds) of soba, and the even larger ‘dekkai’ size has 800 grams (nearly 1.8 pounds). Shortly after ordering, the nikusoba arrived, characterized by its clear golden-hued soup and dark, thick soba. Taking a sip of the soup, it’s a sweet taste and a temperature that isn’t ice-cold as you might expect, but rather around ‘lukewarm’. The soba has the chewiness it looks like it would have—the type you savor by chewing rather than for how smoothly it goes down the throat. This soba, ground from the buckwheat seed together with its inner husk, is in stark contrast to the thin, white noodles you’ll often see at other places in Tokyo. The chicken also has a firm, dense texture, and the more you chew it, the more the flavor comes out. The richly seasoned gesoten complemented the rest of the dish so well, P.K. couldn’t imagine ever having the dish without it as a topping. Soba tends to carry a refined, elegant image in Japan, yet the chewiness and bursting flavors of Toshichi’s nikusoba was a bowl that was endlessly wild . Being open for only three hours on weekdays is a high hurdle to clear for a lot of people, but even so, having a place where you can eat nikusoba without going all the way to Sendai is something to be grateful for. Yamagata soba is a wild soba hiding tremendous potential, so if you find yourself in Tokyo on a weekday around lunchtime, loosen your belt, and go conquer a mountain of glorious, chewy buckwheat. Shop information Nikusoba Toshichi Hanzomon-ten / 肉そば藤七 半蔵門店 Address: Tokyo-to, Chiyoda-ku, Hirakawacho 2-12, Fujimori-biru 1F 東京都千代田区平河町2-12 藤森ビル 1F Open: 11:00 a.m.–2:00 p.m. Closed: Saturdays, Sundays, and national holidays Website Related: Nikusoba Toshichi , Sarashina Horii Photos ©SoraNews24 ● Want to hear about SoraNews24’s latest articles as soon as they’re published? title: Krispy Kreme Japan has a new Year of the Ram donut and one more lucky New Year’s treat
summary: Edible eto. Sometimes, Japanese can be a wonderfully concise language. For example, when talking about the representative animals for each year in traditional Asian divination, in English you’d need to say “Chinese Zodiac animals.” In Japanese, though, you can get the same job done with just two syllables, since the members of that zoological Zodiac […]
details: Edible eto . Sometimes, Japanese can be a wonderfully concise language. For example, when talking about the representative animals for each year in traditional Asian divination, in English you’d need to say “Chinese Zodiac animals.” In Japanese, though, you can get the same job done with just two syllables, since the members of that zoological Zodiac set are called eto . Now, maybe you don’t find yourself discussing the Chinese Zodiac animals all that often, but when an occasion does arise in which you need to tell people something about them as quickly as possible, eto is a word you’ll be glad to know. For instance, right now we need to tell you that Krispy Kreme Japan has a new eto donut on the way! The donut chain has just revealed its new Hitsuji Vanilla Cream donut, with hitusji being the Japanese word for both ram and sheep (told you it can be a concise language). This adorable treat has a white chocolate coating , but while it might look fluffy, it’s actually going to have a lot of crunch to it. In addition to the white chocolate crunch sprinkled across it, it has hazelnuts for the tuft of “wool” on its forehead, and chocolate pieces for the ears, eyes, and mouth. Waiting inside the donut is a sweet milky vanilla cream filling. Unlike most other parts of Asia, Japan changes over to the new eto animal on January 1, so the Hitsuji Vanilla Cream is going to be going on sale in late December, on the 26th, to be precise . The Year of the Ram dessert will be joined from the same day by another New Year’s-themed donut, the Lucky Strawberry . Red and white are the traditional New Year’s colors in Japan, seen as an auspicious combination full of fortuitous portents for the months to come. That might seem a bit lofty in terms of ambitions for a donut, but strawberry fans will no doubt feel like things are going their way as they bite into the white chocolate-covered coating with a strawberry nappage glaze . The sprinkling of freeze-dried strawberry bits where the two lines of white chocolate meet are meant to conjure up thoughts of a mizuhiki , the coiled cord decorations customarily put up for New Year’s in Japan. The Hitsuji Vanilla Cream is priced at 440 yen (US$2.75) and the Lucky Strawberry at 341 yen, and they’re both scheduled to be on sale until January 12 . For that same availability period (December 26-January 12), they can also be purchased as part of an Eto Dozen (3,300 yen), Eto Half-dozen (1,804 yen), or three-donut Eto Box (1,144 yen), accompanied by assortments of other Krispy Kreme donuts, including the chocolate-cream filled Chocolate Snowman with its strawberry-glaze scarf. Oh, and don’t worry, the 396-yen Chocolate Snowman will also be available to spend Christmas with you, as it goes on sale December 1 . title: Bus driver fired for licking inside of the bus during livestream
summary: He’s going to have problems in his next job interviews. Being a bus driver is a difficult job, and having to get a massive vehicle through the often tight and packed streets of Japan every day is bound to take a mental toll. It’s enough to make someone want to just let go and lick […]
details: He’s going to have problems in his next job interviews. Being a bus driver is a difficult job, and having to get a massive vehicle through the often tight and packed streets of Japan every day is bound to take a mental toll. It’s enough to make someone want to just let go and lick the interior of public transportation. Well, it’s enough with the help of a livestreamer egging them on at least. That’s what happened according to Keikyu Bus and the many people who watched it live online. On 16 November, an unidentified bus driver appeared on a livestream of a young woman named Riakyun and was asked by her to lick the handrail and hand strap of his bus after it went out of service for the day . Video and images of it began to circulate on social media, causing the driver to apparently see the saliva-coated writing on the wall and report himself to his employers at Keikyu Bus. On 18 November, Keikyu issued a public apology and promised to take the appropriate actions. Then, on 20 November, they announced that the bus in question had been identified and thoroughly disinfected, and that the driver had been relieved of his duties . Meanwhile, readers of the news online largely felt that Mother Nature has some further penalties in store for this driver. They’re likely right too. Studies have shown that he’d have been taking less of a risk licking a public toilet seat than a public railing. “Wouldn’t you catch the flu from doing that?” “Just, wow…” “Seeing it was even grosser than I imagined.” “Why are people watching this?” “Is he trying to build up his immune system?” “Maybe he’s replenishing his salt intake.” “I’m more worried about that guy’s health than grossed out.” “He’s like a yokai.” “I wouldn’t even touch those things with my hand.” “He clearly loves buses. Give him a raise!” “The woman told him to do it, though.” I don’t think Keikyu Bus has the authority to fire the streamer. They probably could file some sort of lawsuit for the cost of cleaning, but I imagine they’d rather just put this all behind them as soon as possible. They also promised to thoroughly train and instruct all drivers to prevent this from happening again. So, let us take a moment to send our thoughts and prayers to the biggest victims of this incident: all the other bus drivers who now have to attend a seminar telling them not to lick the inside of their buses. title: Bear Proof Cider invites everyone to drink their bears away
summary: “More cider, less bears” is a slogan we can all get behind. They say alcohol never solves anything, but three companies in Japan beg to differ. On 19 November, Oni-Farm, Havas Japan K.K., and Sunny Side Up released Bear Proof Cider, an alcoholic beverage created with the goal of reducing the number of encounters between […]
details: “ More cider, less bears ” is a slogan we can all get behind. They say alcohol never solves anything, but three companies in Japan beg to differ. On 19 November, Oni-Farm, Havas Japan K.K., and Sunny Side Up released Bear Proof Cider, an alcoholic beverage created with the goal of reducing the number of encounters between people and bears in Japan . The number of bear sightings and attacks has risen dramatically in Japan over the past few years, so much so that the Kanji of the Year for 2025 was “bear.” A driving factor of this problem has been steadily declining populations in rural areas, including aging farmers abandoning their land as they become unable to care for it any longer. These now-empty lots, where food still grows wildly, attract hungry bears from the mountains. This further emboldens the bears to venture deeper into human habitats in search of food, and that’s where the problems begin. For example, the northern prefecture of Aomori is famous for its production of apples , but among the millions that go to market each year, many are deemed substandard or have simply fallen by the wayside. This makes Aomori’s orchards veritable bear magnets. ▼ This photo of a bear pilfering apples was taken by Oni Farm, who know the problem firsthand. Bear Proof Cider makes use of these otherwise unusable apples by brewing them into a delicious drink with seven percent alcohol. By using up as many of the apples as possible, the incentive for bears to wander into orchards is reduced, so the more cider we drink, the lower the risk of bears becomes . That’s not the limit of what Bear Proof Cider is doing about this issue either. Oni Farm will use the proceeds from sales of it to improve the state of abandoned farms and ensure they don’t become hideouts or conduits for bears and other wild animals. Currently, it is only sold in the cities of Tokyo and Hirosaki, Aomori , and if you want to find some in either of these places, it’ll be important to know how this works in Japanese. If you go into a shop and ask for some “cider” or “ saida ” in Japanese, you’ll likely be handed a bottle of Sprite. This is because the first carbonated soft drink imported by Japan was a non-alcoholic sparkling apple cider from England. As the drink caught on, “cider” became shorthand for a sweet carbonated drink, particularly the lemon-lime variety , rather than an apple-based beverage. However, there is also apple cider in Japan, but that is pronounced as “ shidoru ” which is based on the French name of “ cidre .” So, when asking the staff of a shop for this drink, remember to pronounce it as “ she-doh-roo .” So, get out there and do your part in keeping bears away from people by getting a buzz on with Bear Proof Cider. It’s not just fun, it could potentially save the lives of both people and bears. Source, images: PR Times ● Want to hear about SoraNews24’s latest articles as soon as they’re published?
