title: My Death Flags Show No Sign of Ending tendrá anime y su villano no quiere morir
summary: My Death Flags Show No Sign of Ending tendrá anime en 2027. Un universitario despierta como el villano de su videojuego favorito y debe evitar su muerte.
details: Anime My Death Flags Show No Sign of Ending tendrá anime y su villano no quiere morir Un universitario despertará dentro de su videojuego favorito, pero como el villano destinado a morir. Jin hace 3 horas 1 Comentarios ADS Imagínate despertar dentro de tu videojuego favorito y descubrir que no eres el héroe, sino uno de los villanos que inevitablemente termina muerto. Pues esa es la pésima suerte del protagonista de My Death Flags Show No Sign of Ending , la popular historia de fantasía escrita por Izumi que finalmente dará el salto a la animación. La editorial Manga Box confirmó que la obra tendrá una adaptación al anime para televisión en 2027 , acompañando el anuncio con una ilustración especial para celebrar la noticia. La serie, conocida en Japón como Ore no Shibou Flag ga Todomaru Tokoro o Shiranai , ya supera 1.75 millones de copias en circulación entre sus novelas y adaptación al manga. Y parece que esa popularidad finalmente consiguió que los responsables se animaran a llevar a la pantalla las desgracias de un protagonista que solamente quiere llegar vivo al final de la historia. Conoce el videojuego de memoria, pero le tocó ser uno de sus villanos La historia sigue a Kazuki Hirasawa , un universitario común y corriente que un día despierta dentro del mundo de Brave Hearts , un videojuego al que había dedicado incontables horas. Sin embargo, en lugar de convertirse en el héroe de la aventura, descubre que ahora ocupa el cuerpo de Harold Stokes , un personaje malvado que está destinado a morir a manos del grupo protagonista. El problema es que Kazuki conoce perfectamente lo que le espera si los acontecimientos siguen el mismo camino que en el juego. Por eso, decide aprovechar todos sus conocimientos para esquivar las numerosas banderas de muerte que rodean a Harold y encontrar una manera de sobrevivir. Por suerte, tampoco está completamente indefenso. Harold es uno de los personajes más poderosos de Brave Hearts , así que Kazuki dispone de habilidades extraordinarias para intentar cambiar su destino. Eso sí, tener fuerza suficiente para enfrentarse a los héroes no significa que resulte sencillo escapar de una historia que parece empeñada en matarlo. Otro de los atractivos de la obra es la peculiar personalidad del protagonista, quien debe desenvolverse con la reputación de un villano arrogante mientras intenta evitar las tragedias que conoce de antemano. De hecho, los responsables destacan su comportamiento tsundere como una de las características que más han conquistado a los lectores. Para celebrar la adaptación, Mitsuya Otosu, ilustrador de la versión manga, preparó una imagen conmemorativa . El autor original, Izumi, también compartió un mensaje agradeciendo el apoyo de los seguidores y expresando su deseo de que el anime permita que nuevas personas descubran la historia. Cabe recordar que My Death Flags Show No Sign of Ending comenzó su publicación en 2014 dentro de la plataforma de novelas web Shosetsuka ni Narou . La obra consiguió el gran premio de la tercera edición del concurso Narou-Con en 2015, lo que impulsó su publicación como novela ligera bajo el sello Takarajimasha, con ilustraciones de A-chiki. Posteriormente, en junio de 2020, comenzó su adaptación al manga ilustrada por Mitsuya Otosu a través de la aplicación Manga Box. Desde entonces, la franquicia ha continuado ganando seguidores hasta superar los 1.75 millones de ejemplares contabilizados entre sus diferentes formatos en octubre de 2026. Por ahora, solamente se ha confirmado que el anime se estrenará en algún momento de 2027 . title: Mashle ya tiene fecha para su temporada 3: los músculos vuelven a desafiar a la magia
summary: Mashle: Magic and Muscles revela un nuevo tráiler y confirma su tercera temporada para enero de 2027. Mash enfrentará nuevos rivales en el examen final.
details: Anime Mashle ya tiene fecha para su temporada 3: los músculos vuelven a desafiar a la magia Mash enfrentará a nuevos rivales en el examen final para convertirse en Visionario Divino. Kudasai hace 1 hora 1 Comentarios ADS Después de demostrar que unos buenos músculos pueden ser más útiles que cualquier hechizo, Mash Burnedead está listo para enfrentarse a nuevos enemigos. Se confirmó oficialmente que la tercera temporada de Mashle: Magic and Muscles se estrenará el 10 de enero de 2027 a la medianoche en Japón , acompañada de un nuevo tráiler y una imagen promocional que adelantan los próximos desafíos de nuestro protagonista. Y parece que esta vez no bastará con levantar pesas y comer profiteroles para salir de todos los problemas. El anuncio se realizó este 11 de noviembre, coincidiendo con el cumpleaños de Mash. La nueva temporada adaptará el arco del examen final para convertirse en Visionario Divino , donde los estudiantes de la Academia de Magia Easton deberán enfrentarse a nuevos y poderosos rivales de la Escuela de Magia Valkis. La imagen promocional muestra a Mash y sus compañeros frente a los integrantes de la escuela rival, mientras que el avance presenta algunas de las batallas que tendrán lugar durante el examen. También se publicaron nuevas ilustraciones individuales de los cinco integrantes principales del dormitorio Adler, que regresarán para acompañar al protagonista durante esta etapa. Mashle presenta a dos nuevos rivales para su tercera temporada Una de las novedades más importantes es la incorporación de Domina Blowlive y Lévis Rosequartz , dos estudiantes de Valkis que tendrán un papel importante en los próximos enfrentamientos. Ambos aparecen en el nuevo tráiler y ya se confirmaron los actores que les darán voz. Soma Saito interpretará a Domina Blowlive , mientras que Ryota Suzuki será Lévis Rosequartz . Este último adelantó que su personaje tiene una personalidad bastante desagradable, pero también posee una enorme fuerza que respalda su arrogancia. Así que Mash tendrá que prepararse para lidiar con otro estudiante convencido de que su poder mágico lo hace superior a los demás. En cuanto a la producción, Tomonari Tanaka regresará como director en A-1 Pictures , acompañado de Yosuke Kuroda en la composición y los guiones de la serie. Chiaki Furuzumi se encargará del diseño de personajes, mientras que Masaru Yokoyama continuará componiendo la banda sonora. La tercera temporada también llegará a Crunchyroll , que confirmó su distribución internacional, incluyendo Latinoamérica, como parte de su programación de invierno de 2027. En Japón, la emisión comenzará a las 00:00 horas del 10 de enero en Tokyo MX, BS11 y otras cadenas, horario que las televisoras japonesas anuncian como las 24:00 del sábado 9 de enero. Cabe recordar que Mashle: Magic and Muscles estrenó su primera temporada en abril de 2023, seguida de una segunda entrega en enero de 2024. La franquicia adapta el manga de Hajime Komoto, publicado en Weekly Shonen Jump entre enero de 2020 y julio de 2023, con un total de 18 volúmenes recopilatorios . La historia sigue a Mash Burnedead, un muchacho que nació sin magia en un mundo donde prácticamente todo depende de ella. Para sobrevivir y proteger su tranquila vida, decide ingresar a una prestigiosa escuela de hechicería y convertirse en Visionario Divino, aunque su única herramienta para superar los desafíos sean sus músculos absurdamente desarrollados. ¿Crees que los nuevos estudiantes de Valkis conseguirán poner a Mash contra las cuerdas, o terminarán descubriendo que ninguna cantidad de magia puede competir contra un buen entrenamiento de pecho y bíceps? title: Nanatsu-ya tendrá anime: una chica puede ver los secretos de las joyas
summary: Nanatsu-ya: Shinobu and Her Jewelry Box tendrá anime en 2027. La obra de la autora de Nodame Cantabile presentó su primer tráiler y equipo de producción.
details: Anime Nanatsu-ya tendrá anime: una chica puede ver los secretos de las joyas La autora de Nodame Cantabile regresa al anime con una historia de misterio, romance y piedras preciosas. Mirukaru hace 1 hora 1 Comentarios ADS Hay personas que pueden reconocer una joya auténtica con solo mirarla, pero Shinobu Kurata lleva ese talento a otro nivel: literalmente puede ver la energía que esconden las piedras preciosas. Y pronto podremos conocer su historia en televisión, pues se anunció que Nanatsu-ya: Shinobu and Her Jewelry Box tendrá una adaptación al anime en 2027 . La obra de Tomoko Ninomiya, creadora de Nodame Cantabile , presentó su primer tráiler y una imagen promocional para celebrar la noticia. El anuncio se realizó este 11 de noviembre, coincidiendo con el Día de la Joyería en Japón. La ilustración muestra a los protagonistas, Shinobu y Akisada, rodeados de piedras preciosas, mientras que el avance destaca los distintos colores y brillos de las joyas que tendrán tanta importancia en la historia. Además, la autora compartió una ilustración especial para celebrar que su manga finalmente llegará a la animación. La historia de Nanatsu-ya: Shinobu and Her Jewelry Box , conocida en Japón como Nanatsuya Shinobu no Hōsekibako , sigue a Shinobu Kurata , una estudiante de preparatoria que ayuda en Kurata-ya, la tradicional casa de empeños de su familia ubicada en uno de los barrios antiguos de Tokio. Aunque todavía es bastante joven, Shinobu posee una habilidad extraordinaria: puede percibir el aura de las piedras preciosas . Gracias a este talento, es capaz de reconocer la verdadera naturaleza de las joyas que llegan al establecimiento, incluso cuando sus características no resultan evidentes para los demás. Pero las piedras preciosas no son lo único complicado en su vida. Resulta que su abuelo decidió comprometerla en matrimonio con Akisada Kitagami, un joven que pertenece a una familia distinguida y que trabaja para una prestigiosa joyería. Y aunque cualquiera pensaría que tener un prometido con semejantes conexiones podría ser bastante conveniente para el negocio familiar, la relación entre ambos tiene una historia mucho más peculiar. Akisada fue acogido por la familia de Shinobu cuando era pequeño, después de separarse de sus propios familiares bajo circunstancias misteriosas. Ahora, mientras trabaja en el mundo de las joyas, continúa buscando respuestas sobre su pasado y los secretos que rodean a su familia. Así, la historia combina los misterios detrás de distintas piedras preciosas, las vidas de quienes llegan a la casa de empeños y la peculiar relación entre sus protagonistas . Porque aparentemente, descubrir cuánto vale un diamante puede ser mucho más sencillo que comprender los sentimientos de una persona. El equipo de Nodame Cantabile vuelve a trabajar con Tomoko Ninomiya Una de las sorpresas del anuncio es que Chiaki Kon dirigirá la adaptación en J.C.STAFF , reuniendo nuevamente a parte del equipo que trabajó en el anime de Nodame Cantabile . Kon estuvo al frente de Nodame Cantabile: Paris Chapter y Nodame Cantabile: Finale , mientras que J.C.STAFF también produjo las temporadas animadas de aquella franquicia. La composición de la serie estará a cargo de Seishi Minakami, conocido por su participación en A Certain Scientific Railgun , mientras que Mai Furuki se encargará del diseño de personajes. En un mensaje compartido durante el anuncio, Kon expresó su alegría por tener otra oportunidad de trabajar en una obra de Ninomiya. La directora también adelantó que espera trasladar a la animación las diferentes historias que comienzan con cada piedra preciosa, conservando el encanto que caracteriza al manga. Cabe recordar que Nanatsu-ya: Shinobu and Her Jewelry Box comenzó a publicarse en noviembre de 2013 dentro de la revista Kiss de Kodansha, donde continúa en serialización. La obra cuenta actualmente con 27 volúmenes recopilatorios , mientras que el volumen 28 llegará a las tiendas japonesas el próximo 13 de noviembre. Por ahora, el estreno solamente está confirmado para algún momento de 2027 , sin una fecha exacta, elenco de voces ni plataformas de distribución internacional anunciadas. Mientras tanto, los lectores del manga finalmente podrán imaginar cómo lucirán las misteriosas auras que Shinobu lleva tantos años observando. ¿Te gustaría tener la habilidad de Shinobu para descubrir los secretos de cualquier joya, o preferirías utilizarla para encontrar una piedra preciosa que te permita hacerte rico sin tener que trabajar? title: En VRChat, un hombre pasa hasta 15 horas al día como chica anime y explica por qué
summary: Un reportaje de ABEMA revela por qué tantos hombres utilizan avatares de chicas anime en VRChat y presenta el caso de un usuario que pasa hasta 15 horas allí.
details: Cultura Otaku En VRChat, un hombre pasa hasta 15 horas al día como chica anime y explica por qué Un reportaje de ABEMA revela por qué tantos hombres prefieren usar avatares femeninos en el mundo virtual. Jin hace 2 horas 4 Comentarios ADS En internet puedes convertirte prácticamente en cualquier cosa, así que no debería sorprendernos que muchos hombres prefieran pasar su tiempo libre convertidos en lindas chicas de anime. Sin embargo, para algunos esta experiencia va mucho más allá de utilizar un personaje bonito. Un reportaje del programa japonés ABEMA Prime presentó el caso de un hombre de treinta y tantos años que pasa hasta 15 horas al día en VRChat utilizando un avatar femenino , mientras una encuesta citada durante la emisión señala que aproximadamente siete de cada diez hombres consultados prefieren este tipo de personajes. Uno de los entrevistados fue Kane , un hombre que lleva siete años utilizando avatares de chicas dentro de esta plataforma de realidad virtual. Aunque su personaje tiene la apariencia de una joven adorable, él no intenta ocultar que es hombre y tampoco modifica su voz para parecer una mujer. Simplemente considera que esa apariencia representa mejor lo que le gusta y la manera en que desea expresarse. Según explicó, siempre ha sentido una gran fascinación por las cosas lindas. De hecho, antes soñaba con convertirse en un hombre musculoso y atractivo, pero con el tiempo descubrió que prefería experimentar una apariencia completamente diferente. Para él, el mayor atractivo de VRChat es poder convertirse en la versión de sí mismo que realmente desea mostrar , sin preocuparse demasiado por las expectativas de quienes lo rodean. Y no estamos hablando de alguien que entra durante unos minutos para conversar. Kane contó que, durante sus días libres, puede permanecer hasta 15 horas dentro del mundo virtual . Como la plataforma también le permite realizar tareas frente a una computadora, aprovecha ese tiempo para trabajar en sus propios proyectos, conversar con amigos y participar en diferentes actividades. En la vida real tiene un empleo de atención al público, por lo que continúa alternando ambas experiencias. La práctica es conocida en Japón como babíniku , una abreviatura de virtual bishoujo juniku , que hace referencia a adoptar la apariencia de una hermosa chica dentro de un entorno virtual. Aunque suele asociarse con hombres que utilizan personajes femeninos, sus motivaciones pueden ser bastante diferentes y no necesariamente están relacionadas con su identidad de género. Para explicar el fenómeno, el programa también entrevistó a Nemu , una VTuber especializada en la cultura del metaverso que lleva aproximadamente diez años participando en estas comunidades. Según explicó, existen dos razones especialmente frecuentes para elegir avatares femeninos: la variedad de opciones de personalización y la facilidad para relacionarse con otras personas . En primer lugar, los personajes femeninos suelen contar con una oferta mucho más amplia de ropa, peinados y accesorios, especialmente cuando se busca una estética adorable. Esto permite a los usuarios experimentar con estilos que difícilmente podrían utilizar en su vida cotidiana. Además, Nemu señaló que los avatares con apariencia femenina pueden facilitar determinadas interacciones sociales, pues algunas personas sienten que resulta más sencillo acercarse y entablar amistades con ellos. La especialista también aclaró que utilizar un avatar femenino no significa automáticamente que la persona sea transgénero . Aunque existen usuarios que exploran cuestiones relacionadas con su identidad, los estudios que mencionó indican que esa no es la motivación predominante entre los hombres que adoptan personajes femeninos. De acuerdo con una encuesta sobre usuarios de realidad virtual social citada en el programa, alrededor del 70 por ciento de los hombres participantes utilizaba avatares femeninos . Eso sí, la cifra corresponde a los encuestados y no significa que siete de cada diez hombres de internet, o necesariamente de toda la comunidad de VRChat , tengan esa preferencia. El problema llega cuando toca regresar al mundo real Sin embargo, Kane también reconoció que su experiencia tiene momentos difíciles. Después de pasar tantas horas utilizando la apariencia que más le gusta, regresar a la realidad y encontrarse con su imagen frente al espejo puede resultarle incómodo. Según explicó, a veces le cuesta aceptar la diferencia entre cómo se ve dentro del mundo virtual y su aspecto físico cotidiano. También admitió que se ha distanciado de algunas amistades de la vida real , pues no siempre consigue mantener el mismo equilibrio entre ambos espacios. Nemu, por su parte, aseguró que vive las dos experiencias de manera separada y disfruta tanto de sus relaciones fuera de internet como de las amistades que ha construido dentro del metaverso. El reportaje mostró así que, para algunos usuarios, VRChat no es solamente un videojuego donde puedes disfrazarte de waifu. También puede convertirse en un espacio para probar otras formas de presentarse ante los demás, conocer personas y disfrutar de una apariencia que sería imposible mantener en la vida cotidiana. ¿Si pudieras pasar el día entero dentro de VRChat , elegirías un avatar parecido a ti o aprovecharías para convertirte en una chica de anime completamente diferente? title: Chained Soldier retrasa su regreso por la lesión de su ilustrador
summary: Yōhei Takemura todavía se recupera de una lesión en la muñeca, por lo que el manga regresará en diciembre.
details: Manga Chained Soldier retrasa su regreso por la lesión de su ilustrador Yōhei Takemura todavía se recupera de una lesión en la muñeca, por lo que el manga regresará en diciembre. Kudasai hace 33 minutos 0 Comentarios ADS Los fanáticos de Chained Soldier tendrán que esperar un poco más para descubrir cómo continúa la historia de Yuuki y las integrantes de la Fuerza de Defensa Demoníaca. La cuenta oficial de Shonen Jump+ anunció que el manga retrasará su regreso hasta el 12 de diciembre de 2026 , debido a que su ilustrador, Yōhei Takemura, todavía se encuentra recuperándose de una lesión en la muñeca derecha. Originalmente, la obra tenía previsto reanudar su publicación el 14 de noviembre, después de entrar en pausa durante octubre. Sin embargo, los responsables decidieron concederle más tiempo al artista para evitar que sus problemas físicos empeoren. La buena noticia es que, según el nuevo comunicado, Takemura ya retomó sus labores de dibujo , aunque la editorial considera necesario mantener el descanso de la serialización durante algunas semanas adicionales. La situación comenzó en junio de este año, cuando Takemura sufrió una lesión en la muñeca derecha que afectó el fibrocartílago, un tejido importante para el movimiento y la estabilidad de esta articulación. A pesar del problema, continuó dibujando los capítulos del manga utilizando una muñequera para intentar reducir las molestias. Lamentablemente, las largas jornadas de dibujo terminaron dificultando su recuperación. El propio artista explicó anteriormente que el uso constante de la mano provocaba dolor y que la lesión necesitaba más tiempo para sanar. Por ello, decidió interrumpir temporalmente la elaboración de los manuscritos y concentrarse en su tratamiento. Cuando se anunció la pausa original, el equipo editorial de Shonen Jump+ aseguró que la recuperación de Takemura sería la máxima prioridad . También explicó que cualquier decisión sobre el ritmo de publicación se tomaría en conjunto con el guionista Takahiro y siguiendo las recomendaciones médicas. Ahora, con el nuevo aplazamiento, se espera que el capítulo 189 llegue el sábado 12 de diciembre . La fecha sigue siendo una previsión de la editorial, por lo que podría modificarse si la recuperación del ilustrador lo requiere. Para quienes no estén familiarizados con la franquicia, Chained Soldier , conocido en Japón como Mato Seihei no Slave , es un manga escrito por Takahiro e ilustrado por Yōhei Takemura que comenzó a publicarse en enero de 2019 a través de Shonen Jump+ . La historia se desarrolla en un mundo donde misteriosos portales conectan Japón con una dimensión habitada por monstruos llamados Shuuki. En ese lugar crecen unos duraznos especiales que otorgan poderes sobrenaturales, aunque solamente funcionan en las mujeres. Por eso, la humanidad depende de una organización femenina encargada de combatir a estas criaturas. El protagonista es Yuuki Wakura , un estudiante que termina encontrándose con Kyouka Uzen, capitana del séptimo escuadrón de la Fuerza de Defensa Demoníaca. Después de descubrir que puede transformarse en una poderosa arma bajo sus órdenes, comienza una vida bastante peculiar donde las batallas sobrenaturales vienen acompañadas de recompensas que no siempre resultan apropiadas para todos los públicos. La franquicia recibió su primera adaptación al anime en enero de 2024, seguida de una segunda temporada estrenada en enero de 2026. Además, una tercera temporada ya se encuentra anunciada , aunque todavía no tiene fecha de estreno confirmada. Por ahora, los lectores tendrán que esperar hasta diciembre para reencontrarse con el manga. Al menos, el nuevo comunicado confirma que Takemura ha podido retomar parte de su trabajo, mientras la editorial continúa tomando precauciones para que su recuperación no se vea perjudicada. ¿Prefieres que Chained Soldier se tome todo el tiempo necesario para que Takemura se recupere, aunque eso signifique esperar varios meses más por los próximos capítulos? title: MAPPA suma un poderoso aliado: CyberAgent compra parte de su empresa matriz
summary: CyberAgent compra parte de la empresa matriz de MAPPA y anuncia una alianza para desarrollar anime, videojuegos, productos y eventos a nivel internacional.
details: Anime MAPPA suma un poderoso aliado: CyberAgent compra parte de su empresa matriz La compañía detrás de ABEMA y Cygames colaborará con el estudio en anime, videojuegos, productos y eventos. Jin hace 17 segundos 0 Comentarios ADS El estudio detrás de Jujutsu Kaisen y Chainsaw Man acaba de conseguir un nuevo socio con bastante experiencia en la industria del entretenimiento. La compañía japonesa CyberAgent anunció una alianza comercial con MAPPA y confirmó que adquirió parte de las acciones de MHD, la empresa matriz del estudio de animación. El acuerdo fue presentado oficialmente el 11 de noviembre y contempla colaboraciones que van mucho más allá de producir nuevas series de anime. Para quienes no estén familiarizados con CyberAgent, se trata de uno de los grandes grupos de entretenimiento de Japón, responsable de negocios como la plataforma de streaming ABEMA y la desarrolladora de videojuegos Cygames , conocida por franquicias como Uma Musume: Pretty Derby y Granblue Fantasy . Ahora, la compañía busca aprovechar esa experiencia para desarrollar nuevas oportunidades junto a MAPPA. Eso sí, hay un detalle importante: CyberAgent no ha comprado MAPPA por completo . La inversión se realizó mediante la adquisición de una participación en MHD, cuya presidencia también está a cargo de Manabu Otsuka, actual director ejecutivo del estudio. Las empresas no revelaron cuánto dinero estuvo involucrado ni qué porcentaje de las acciones cambió de manos. De acuerdo con el comunicado oficial, la alianza buscará combinar la capacidad de producción de MAPPA con la experiencia comercial de CyberAgent . Esto incluye colaborar desde las primeras etapas de planificación de un anime hasta su distribución internacional, pasando por posibles adaptaciones a videojuegos, productos oficiales y eventos para los seguidores. En otras palabras, ambas compañías quieren participar en más aspectos de una franquicia, en lugar de limitarse a producir una serie y dejar el resto de sus actividades en manos de otras empresas. Sin embargo, todavía no se ha anunciado ningún proyecto concreto como resultado de este acuerdo, por lo que sería prematuro esperar adaptaciones a videojuegos de las producciones más populares de MAPPA. Y aunque el anuncio pueda parecer una colaboración completamente nueva, ambas compañías llevan bastante tiempo trabajando juntas. De hecho, uno de sus primeros proyectos fue Rage of Bahamut: Genesis , anime producido por MAPPA en 2014 a partir del videojuego de Cygames. Desde entonces, también han colaborado en la planificación de otras producciones, su distribución mediante ABEMA y diferentes proyectos relacionados con videojuegos. En una entrevista publicada junto con el anuncio, los presidentes de ambas compañías explicaron que su relación profesional comenzó hace aproximadamente ocho años. Manabu Otsuka, presidente de MAPPA, y Takahiro Yamauchi, presidente de CyberAgent , destacaron que comparten una visión sobre la importancia de cuidar las obras y encontrar mejores maneras de acercarlas al público internacional. Yamauchi señaló que ambas empresas comparten la filosofía Creative First , centrada en respetar el trabajo de los creadores. Por su parte, Otsuka aseguró que MAPPA continuará prestando especial atención a la calidad de sus producciones, mientras aprovecha las fortalezas de su nuevo socio para ampliar las experiencias que puede ofrecer a los espectadores. Por ahora, MAPPA confirmó que mantendrá su estructura administrativa y continuará operando como un estudio de animación independiente . Esto significa que el acuerdo no implica un cambio anunciado en su dirección ni que CyberAgent vaya a tomar automáticamente el control de sus próximas producciones. La alianza forma parte de una tendencia de ambas compañías por ampliar sus actividades alrededor del anime. MAPPA lleva varios años involucrándose más directamente en la gestión comercial de sus obras, mientras CyberAgent ha reforzado sus inversiones en producción animada, videojuegos y distribución de contenidos. Así, el acuerdo podría abrir nuevas oportunidades para desarrollar franquicias y acercarlas a espectadores de otros países. Sin embargo, sus resultados dependerán de los proyectos que las compañías decidan emprender, pues todavía no se conocen nuevas series, películas o videojuegos vinculados específicamente con esta inversión. ¿Qué te gustaría ver primero de esta alianza: un nuevo anime original de MAPPA o un videojuego basado en alguna de sus franquicias más populares? title: Starbucks Japan reveals new Joyful Capsule gacha toy release date
summary: The wait for these Japan-exclusive collectibles is almost over. Back in July, Starbucks surprised customers in Japan with the news that it would be releasing a never-before-seen “Joyful Capsule” collection. Consisting of nine miniature plush charms across two collections, the range is Starbucks’ first-ever gacha capsule toy collection, and though it was first slated to […]
details: The wait for these Japan-exclusive collectibles is almost over. Back in July, Starbucks surprised customers in Japan with the news that it would be releasing a never-before-seen “ Joyful Capsule ” collection. Consisting of nine miniature plush charms across two collections , the range is Starbucks’ first-ever gacha capsule toy collection , and though it was first slated to be released in August, the launch was postponed out of consideration for victims of the 28 July earthquake in Kumamoto Prefecture. Now, Starbucks has announced that the new release date has been set for 18 November , and unlike the previous plan, which limited sales to only 19 Starbucks stores in Tokyo, the standard collection will now be available at stores right around the country . This is great news for Starbucks fans, who have been patiently waiting to get their hands on the collection. Each gacha capsule contains a palm-sized plush charm measuring approximately 5-8 centimetres (2-3 inches), with a handy hook attachment that allows you to easily pop it onto a bag or pouch, or even connect it to other charms in the series. The contents of each capsule are random, so you won’t know which design you’ve got until you open it, and there are five designs in the standard collection , inspired by some of Starbucks’ most recognisable menu items. ▼ Double Tall Latte (To Go) ▼ Caramel Macchiato (For Here) ▼ Tokyo Roast ▼ Matcha Cream Frappuccino ▼ Sugar Doughnut In addition to the standard collection, there will be a special Starbucks Reserve Joyful Capsule range released on the same day at the Starbucks Reserve Roastery Tokyo . This exclusive range features four plush charms inspired by drinks and food items associated with the Roastery , giving fans the chance to take home a little memento of the special store . ▼ Caffe Americano (To Go) ▼ Caffe Latte (For Here) ▼ Tokyo Roastery Microblend ▼ Cornetti Crema While each capsule in the standard range costs 880 yen (US$5.70), the Reserve collection is priced slightly higher, at 1,100 yen each. Whichever collection you choose, though, purchases are limited to two capsules per transaction for each collection , to allow as many customers as possible to own a piece of the collection. The method of sale may also vary between stores, with some using traditional capsule toy machines and others selling the capsules over the counter. The charms are intended for ages 15 and up, and will only be available while stocks last. Source, images: Press release ● Want to hear about SoraNews24’s latest articles as soon as they’re published? title: Is hamburger patty ramen a case of too many good things in one bowl? Let’s find out! [Taste test]
summary: Far away from Japan’s most touristy neighborhoods is a daring fusion dish from a very old-school restaurant. Generally speaking, ramen and hamburger patties are pretty far apart from each other on the eastern-or-western culinary spectrum. Personally, we’re big fans of both here at SoraNews24, but it’s generally sort of an either/or question as to which […]
details: Far away from Japan’s most touristy neighborhoods is a daring fusion dish from a very old-school restaurant . Generally speaking, ramen and hamburger patties are pretty far apart from each other on the eastern-or-western culinary spectrum. Personally, we’re big fans of both here at SoraNews24, but it’s generally sort of an either/or question as to which one of those cravings we’re going to satisfy in single meal. So imagine the surprise of our Japanese-language reporter Takuya Inaba when he recently discovered the existence of hamburger steak ramen . That might sound like the sort of thing you’d encounter at a tourist-trap eatery near downtown Tokyo’s Shibuya crossing, but instead we came across this innovative dish at Koryu , a decidedly old-school ramen restaurant not far from the shore of Lake Sagami in the town of Sagamihara in Kanagawa , the prefecture that borders Tokyo on the capital’s southern side. From its exterior, Koryu (whose name translates as “Lake Dragon”), does not look like a place that chases after gimmicky food trends, and that vibe continues once you step inside. This restaurant has been serving up ramen in this location for roughly 40 years, and it has the sort of rustically inviting, at-home atmosphere that makes you understandingly nod your head at how long it’s been in business . Flipping through the menu, we first saw a page with old standards like shoyu (soy sauce broth) and miso ramen, with prices starting at just 680 yen (US$4.30). But then we got to the section where the more deluxe options are listed, and there it was. ▼ Hamburger steak ramen Fusion recipes like this are always a bit of a gamble, but at a still-reasonable price of 1,080 yen, we decided to roll the dice and order it. As Ryuko’s owner, who operates the restaurant by himself most days, began preparing our hamburger steak ramen, we braced ourselves for an utterly bizarre-looking bowl of noodles to be placed before us… …but it turned out to be shockingly normal looking . Not plain or unappealing, mind you, but largely in keeping with what you’d expect to see in a bowl of ramen, with negi (green onions), menma (fermented bamboo shoots), seaweed , kinshi tamago (thin strands of egg), and a swirly naruto fish cake. Following standard ramen-tasting protocol, Takuya started with a sip of the broth. It was flavorful, with what he describes as strong umami sensations and a mild saltiness which still came to an incredibly clean finish in its flavor profile, leading him to think the pork stock must be made by cooking on low heat for a very long time . OK, now it was time to take a clearer look at the hamburger steak, which Takuya could perceive subtly floating underneath the egg. Using his spoon, he brushed the strands aside. Ah, there you are! Obviously, the hamburger steak didn’t say hi or otherwise audibly announce its presence, but it immediately demanded attention by nature of being something you just don’t see in this environment, like if there had been a polar bear soaking in the broth. However, after the broth the next thing ramen fans say you’re supposed to taste is the noodles, so Takuya did what he could to put the hamburger steak out of his mind for the moment. The noodles, which the owner makes himself in-house, had a nice, springy texture to them, and Takuya was blown away by how good the menma, which the owner also personally prepares, tasted . But at this point, Takuya couldn’t contain his curiosity any longer, so it was time to try the hamburger steak . Balanced on his spoon, he was happily surprised at just how big it was. Now thoroughly soaked with broth, he wondered if this mix of eastern and western elements really could work together, so he took a bite… …and discovered that, yeah, this is honestly good stuff! Unlike with a hamburger or a standard hamburger steak set meal, the patty here isn’t slathered with ketchup, barbecue sauce, or any other condiments. Instead, the delicious flavor of the meat itself is what gets full play on your taste buds, and by nature of being less fatty and oily than many of the chashu pork strips that are the most common meaty topping for ramen, the broth’s inherently appealing flavors aren’t muddled in any way either . So it turns out that just like hamburger patties can work as a sushi topping , they can work as a ramen topping too. Again, since Ryuko is a one-man-run restaurant, waits can get long around peak lunch and dinner hours, so we’d recommend avoiding those times, and the location does mean that experiencing this unique dish for yourself will take a bit of planning, but with the nearby Lake Sagami Illumination Christmas light display making its return later this month, there are two reasons to make the day trip from Tokyo out to this part of Japan. title: Historical-themed illumination display returns to Osaka Castle this winter
summary: The greatest lights in history and the greatest history in lights. I’ve never been too good at history, mainly because I’m terrible at remembering names and dates. But I find when it’s presented in ways other than fact sheets, I can remember what happened a lot more clearly. If you’re like me, then an upcoming […]
details: The greatest lights in history and the greatest history in lights. I’ve never been too good at history, mainly because I’m terrible at remembering names and dates. But I find when it’s presented in ways other than fact sheets, I can remember what happened a lot more clearly. If you’re like me, then an upcoming event in Osaka might be just what you need to handle the long and complex history of Japan. From 20 November to 14 February, the Nishinomaru Garden of Osaka Castle will be brilliantly lit up. Although an illumination display might just sound like a bunch of lights, they tend to go really all out with them in Japan, and the Osaka Castle Illuminage is no exception. This year’s theme is “ Unification of the Realm, Shogun – A Story in Light ,” and boasts almost as many lights as it has subtitles, fittingly using the castle that noted warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi once resided in as a backdrop. In a nutshell, Toyotomi was one of The Three Unifiers of Japan, having worked his way up from the peasant class to grasp control of the entire country. He ordered the construction of Osaka Castle as a base of operations for about a decade before his death in 1598. This illumination event goes far beyond that, however, with an array of dazzling displays both educational and fantastical. Upon entering the garden, guests will follow a corridor of 66 lanterns to help you feel like you’re right in the light show, rather than looking at it from afar. Then, there’s an array of taiko drums , bearing the paulownia crest of the Toyotomi clan, which is still used by the Japanese government today. The drums are meant to be a symbol of the strength the entire country has when working together as one, while also providing the atmosphere of a traditional festival, where these types of drums are often employed. Deeper inside is a light display in the shape of a large nanban trading ship . It is often pointed out that “nanban” literally means “Southern barbarian” and was used for Portuguese traders who successfully reached Japan. However, it was more of a generalized term inherited from Chinese, and many of the goods, arts, and technology brought in by these traders were highly regarded. That’s not to say the “barbarian” label wasn’t used pejoratively as well. There was plenty of discrimination to go around back then too. Speaking of which, the fashions brought in from foreign traders were often well received and had a gradual influence on Japanese culture. It’s something that can be seen in a line of light-based illustrations showcasing how people dressed from 1615 through the large-scale Westernization of Japan in the early 20th century and to the present day. The journey ends at a plaza-like area with neon light displays featuring an assortment of images from Japanese culture , past and present. It’s the perfect place to take a commemorative photo of your visit. This year will also see two new additions to Osaka Castle Illuminage. First, there’s a butterfly swing that is likely to see a lot of action. When rocking back and forth on this four-meter-tall swing set, the wings of the giant butterfly on top move. There’s also a small enclosure that you can enter. Its walls are made of dozens of pinwheels , so when a breeze comes by, they’ll spin and scatter the lights in unexpected patterns. The Osaka Castle Illuminage will be open every day during the period from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. rain or shine. Just remember that although much of Osaka Castle is free to walk around, the Nishinomaru Garden section charges an admission of 2,000 yen (US$13) for adults and 1,000 yen for kids, but babies get in for free. There’s also a really good cake shop nearby if you need to kill some time before it gets dark. Check it out if you can and learn some history or be doomed to repeat it. Just like that guy, whatsisface from the 17th or 18th century. Event information Osaka Castle Illuminage: Unification of the Realm, Shogun – A Story in Light / 大阪城イルミナージュ「天下一統 光の章 SHOGUN 」 Osaka Nishinomaru Garden 大阪城西の丸庭園 Osaka-fu, Osaka-shi, Chuo-ku, Osaka-jo 2 大阪府大阪市中央区大阪城2 Period: 20 November, 2026 – 14 February, 2027 Hours: 5 p.m. – 10 p.m. Admission: Junior High Students and Up – 2,000 yen, Elementary Students and under – 1,000 yen, 1-year-old and Under – Free Website Source, images: PR Times ● Want to hear about SoraNews24’s latest articles as soon as they’re published? title: Japanese drivers reminded to look out for drunk people passed out on the road this holiday season
summary: As if driving in Japan isn’t hard enough. As the year gradually draws to a close, it’s the time for many organizations to hold their year-end parties. Although many younger people have been increasingly distancing themselves from overindulging in alcohol, drinking is still a major part of these year-end festivities. As a result, this is […]
details: As if driving in Japan isn’t hard enough. As the year gradually draws to a close, it’s the time for many organizations to hold their year-end parties . Although many younger people have been increasingly distancing themselves from overindulging in alcohol, drinking is still a major part of these year-end festivities. As a result, this is also the prime time of year to find business people passed out on benches, the side of the road, or, more problematically, right in the middle of roads. People passing out on roads, or “rojo nekomi” as it’s known in Japan, is not new but a lot of attention has been given to it in recent years after people started heading back to the bars in a post-COVID world. In 2023, about 32 percent of nighttime traffic fatalities involving pedestrians in Tokyo were people who fell asleep on the street. However, alcohol shouldn’t take all the blame for this either. According to the National Police Agency, only 70 percent of rojo nekomi incidents were connected to alcohol, with rising temperatures and an aging population leading to other health issues like heatstroke causing people to faint on the road. ▼ The Japan Auto Federation released a video examining how easy it is for drivers to spot and respond to a person sleeping on the road at night. It’s in Japanese but fairly easy to get the gist of, regardless of the language. In response, various taxi companies have begun working hand-in-hand with the police forces of 32 prefectures to keep an eye out for unconscious people on the streets. The programs seem to be effective as well, because on 9 November, a pair of Tokyo cab drivers were officially commended for assisting street sleepers in two separate incidents. Seijo Police Station invited 70-year-old Yoshitatsu Miura and 28-year-old Kazuki Yamamoto to honor their efforts in rescuing two people from potential death . During the ceremony, Miura explained that he encountered the body at about 2 a.m. and shone his headlights on the person to make them highly visible to other motorists while he called the emergency number for help. In Yamamoto’s case, he felt disappointed that while he was helping the unconscious person, there were other people walking along the street at the time. Some just chose to look the other way. Online comments were happy everything turned out fine in these instances, while some admitted they might not have the courage to get involved like these drivers had. “Everyone was lucky this had a happy ending. If the drivers had hit those people, their lives would have been ruined too.” “Papers are nice and all, but give them some money for that!” “I saw an elderly man sleeping on the road while drunk. I asked if he was OK, but he just yelled at me, so I just moved him out of the way and left. From now on, I’m going to ignore anyone I see like that.” “I wonder what the cutoff is for getting commendations? Tons of people report stuff to the police, after all.” “It’s a common thing in Tokyo near the end of the year.” “If you get so drunk that you sleep on the road, then alcohol isn’t for you.” “I don’t want to get involved, so I probably wouldn’t touch them, but I think I could call someone…” “People who get drunk and fall asleep on the street should be penalized too.” Punishing those who fall asleep on the streets due to drunkenness is a tricky issue. Unlike in Western countries, being even extremely drunk in public is not illegal as long as the intoxicated person is not harassing, assaulting, or damaging anyone or anything. If someone is passed out due to alcohol, the police will detain them for their own protection rather than to arrest them for a crime. That being said, obstructing traffic by lying down or sitting on the road is a crime , punishable by a maximum fine of 50,000 yen (US$317). The problem here is that it’s pretty hard to prove intent on the part of the sleeping person if they’re unconscious at the time of the offense. In Okinawa, where the warm climate has helped to make rojo nekomi a more pervasive problem, the police have been more aggressive and have begun charging repeat offenders with traffic obstruction charges. ▼ This news report features harrowing dashcam footage of a driver stopping right in front of a person sleeping on the road in Itoman, Okinawa. As far as civil litigation goes, the liability for damages or injuries that occurred is considered 30 percent the sleeper’s if during the day and 50 percent if at night. But regardless of how these incidents play out, no good comes of it for anyone involved, so stay safe either by drinking in moderation and getting a safe ride home or by driving at a reasonable speed at night with the appropriate lights in use. title: Yakuza boss sues expressway owners for discrimination against criminals
summary: You gotta fight for your right to be a party to a contract. Ever since 2011, things have been getting rougher and rougher for members of organized crime groups in Japan. That was when a law was passed prohibiting companies from entering into contracts with any known member. That’s why any time you sign up […]
details: You gotta fight for your right to be a party to a contract. Ever since 2011, things have been getting rougher and rougher for members of organized crime groups in Japan. That was when a law was passed prohibiting companies from entering into contracts with any known member . That’s why any time you sign up for a phone or point card , you have to declare on it whether or not you belong to such a group. And with just about everything shifting from cash-based purchases to cashless subscriptions, members of groups such as the yakuza are in an increasingly tight situation. One example can be found on Japan’s many privately owned expressways that require a toll to drive on. It is expected that all toll boths will end cash toll payments in favor of the ETC card system by 2030. An ETC card is like an auxiliary credit card that hooks up directly to your car and is detected automatically as you enter and leave an expressway , billing you the appropriate amount. You need to sign up for one much like you do with a credit card, which means yakuza cannot. Feeling his freedom of movement was hindered by this, a senior yakuza member filed a lawsuit against the operators of expressways, such as NEXCO East , for discrimination . According to the suit, in July 2023, the plaintiff attempted to apply for a special ETC Personal Card that doesn’t require a credit card to use, because he can’t get one of those either. On the application was a checkbox that should be marked if the applicant is a member of an organized crime group. The plaintiff just crossed that whole section out and filled in the rest of the application properly. He was notified a month later that his application was denied. On 10 November, a ruling was handed down in Fukuoka District Court, wherein Judge Masakatsu Tange dismissed the lawsuit , saying that by not being able to use expressways, the restrictions on his rights and freedoms were very minor. In Japan, these roads are completely optional, and it is possible to take similar routes to anywhere in the country. The only major benefits are a lack of traffic lights that will generally ensure a swifter arrival than regular city streets. So, the judge is right in that regard. The yakuza member’s ability to go places is more inconvenienced than it is obstructed. ▼ Though in his defense, the sheer number of red lights on regular streets in Japan is rather maddening. There’s a strange kind of irony to see the yakuza trying to settle matters in a court of law. He also has a point that these restrictive laws against people like him are technically discriminatory, but the matter boils down to whether society deems it right to discriminate against criminals or not. Most online comments regarding this story seem to agree that it is right. “Just walk then.” “He’s not really a credible plaintiff, after all.” “Maybe he should just stop doing illegal stuff?” “That’s on him.” “They’re free to leave that life behind, aren’t they?” “What is this guy talking about? It’s not like he follows the law.” “They shouldn’t even be allowed to have driver’s licenses.” “Even with that kind of ETC card, he’d need a bank account, so how did he get that? Or a lawyer, for that matter?” This law prohibiting doing business with organized crime groups was enacted in 2011, meaning before that it was possible for members to open bank accounts and do lots of other things. That’s why you might see a yakuza member using an old flip phone, because they’re contractually stuck in that era’s tech . Also, many people get bank accounts at a young age, likely before they enter a life of crime. As for hiring a lawyer, that is a constitutional right that cannot be denied, so crime groups are allowed to enter into contracts with attorneys as an exception. That’s also why they can receive medical care, which is also a business transaction but guaranteed by law. Public utility providers also cannot refuse service to anyone by law, but yakuza members technically aren’t allowed to buy property, so I’m not sure where they’ll hook it up. Still, it’s definitely a pain in the butt being a member of the yakuza these days, and by design. It just goes to show that all the goons in the world can’t save you from a passive-aggressive bureaucracy. title: KFC Japan starts selling soft-serve ice cream at select locations, and they’ve even put it in a biscuit
summary: There are many ways to enjoy this new sweet dessert, including as a dip for fried chicken. KFC is world-famous for its fried chicken, but right now it’s turning heads for something else in Japan, with the release of soft-serve ice cream. While that would be big news on its own, what’s even more impressive […]
details: There are many ways to enjoy this new sweet dessert, including as a dip for fried chicken. KFC is world-famous for its fried chicken, but right now it’s turning heads for something else in Japan, with the release of soft-serve ice cream . While that would be big news on its own, what’s even more impressive is the fact that the chain is also sandwiching the soft serve inside a biscuit , creating a brand new dessert on the menu. Available only at select locations, we sent our ice-cream-loving reporter Mr Sato over to our nearest participating branch in Tokyo’s Akihabara to check it out as soon as we heard about it. ▼ Upon arriving, he saw this sign outside, which made him think “When the heck did this happen!?” It really is an under-the-radar release , with information about it scarcely available online, and after asking staff about it, Mr Sato learned that sales only began in late October . Though Mr Sato thought it was a shame that sales hadn’t begun earlier in summer, he certainly wasn’t complaining, and after mulling over the three soft serve cones available – vanilla , chocolate and a mix of both for 290 yen (US$1.81) each – he decided to opt for the “ Biscuit & Soft-Serve Drink Set ” for 680 yen. After placing his order, Mr Sato began to fret as he realised that the warm biscuit might make the soft serve melt faster than usual, which isn’t ideal for someone with the responsibility of photographing the dessert. Determined to get the best photos possible, he rubbed his hands together and prepared his fingers for some fast snapping, which meant that when it arrived, he was ready to grab a selfie with the new dessert. Wasting no time, he turned the camera back towards the dessert, which looked gloriously sinful, but peering closer, he realised that… ▼ …the ice cream already seemed to be melting from the heat of the biscuit. As an experienced soft-serve eater, Mr Sato knows that a variety of factors affect the melting rate of ice cream, including the milk fat content and the amount of air incorporated into it. With this variety looking both milky and airy, he had little time to waste, so he dipped his spoon in for a taste. The flavour was very simple and not particularly strong, giving him neither an especially good nor bad impression. Personally, he thought that Family Mart’s soft-serve actually had more flavour, and was an arguably better deal at just 298 yen, even for the Giga Size. ▼ Still, the creaminess was great, and the ice cream isn’t designed to be eaten on its own, so he tried it with the biscuit. The combination of warm, crispy biscuit and soft-serve ice cream was a winning one. The contrast between crunchiness and meltiness was irresistible, and though you can eat them together as a sort of ice cream sandwich, he found that dipping the biscuit into the soft-serve proved to be another great way to enjoy it. Using the soft serve as a dip turned out to be such a good idea that he decided to try it with some of the other items on the menu. ▼ French fry and soft serve = heaven. After trying the chip dip, it was time to move onto bigger fry, quite literally, with a fried chicken dip. You’d be forgiven for thinking Mr Sato may have gone too far with this idea, but he genuinely recommends giving this combination a try. The sweetness of the cream brings out the savoury saltiness and spices of the chicken, making it taste even better. This unusual but delicious combo reminded Mr Sato of chicken and waffles – popular in the American South, the home of fried chicken – which combines fried chicken with maple syrup. ▼ That thought reminded him that the dessert came with honey maple syrup, so he wasted no time in pouring it over. ▼ The soft serve was now disappearing fast, so after snapping a couple of shots… ▼…he dipped his spoon in for a taste. Though he’d now finished his chicken, so was unable to try it with the honey maple syrup-enhanced ice cream, the drizzle of sweet sauce elevated everything into pure dessert territory. The slightly sweet biscuit, sweet soft-serve and added sweetness from the honey maple syrup created the ultimate triple-sweet treat. Mr Sato dialled up the bliss levels by enjoying it all with a hot coffee on the side, which helped to create the ultimate dessert experience. Trying the soft serve multiple ways is the key to ultimate enjoyment, and Mr Sato highly recommends trying it if you can. As of now, Mr Sato was able to confirm that the soft-serve is currently available at the Akihabara and Asakusa branches in Tokyo, as well as the Minami-machida Grandberry Park branch. There doesn’t appear to be any official information about the rollout, so he recommends checking social media and confirming availability with each branch before visiting. Anime and manga have become hugely popular around the world, introducing millions of people to Japanese culture and encouraging many to learn the language themselves. Now, the Japanese government is hoping to capitalize on that popularity with an app that makes learning Japanese feel more like interacting with your favorite characters. Article continues after ad Japan wants anime characters to teach you Japanese As reported by The Japan Times , Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has asked the Japan Foundation to develop an AI-powered language-learning app aimed primarily at younger audiences overseas. Rather than simply studying vocabulary or completing exercises, users would be able to practice speaking Japanese by having conversations with characters from popular anime and manga. While no specific characters or franchises have been announced just yet, it would likely mean users could converse with the likes of Goku from Dragon Ball Z or Monkey D. Luffy from One Piece . The government hopes the app will encourage more people to learn Japanese while also making lessons accessible in countries where qualified teachers and dedicated language schools are harder to find. It could also give anime fans a new way to engage with the characters they love, although they’ll have to wait to find out which ones will be available. title: Tokyo neighborhood adds new “smart trash cans” to deal with increasing amounts of tourist litter
summary: A high-tech part of Tokyo gets some high-tech help in addressing an overtourism problem and responding to a common traveler complaint. Downtown Tokyo’s Akihabara neighborhood is already one of the most popular tourism destinations for travelers in Japan, by nature of being the country’s center of anime and video game fan culture, and a couple […]
details: A high-tech part of Tokyo gets some high-tech help in addressing an overtourism problem and responding to a common traveler complaint . Downtown Tokyo’s Akihabara neighborhood is already one of the most popular tourism destinations for travelers in Japan, by nature of being the country’s center of anime and video game fan culture, and a couple of new additions to the district are sure to be instant crowd pleasers too. We’re not talking about a new multi-level arcade or manga merch specialty store, though, but a bunch of new public trash cans . Japan’s relative lack of trash receptacles in public spaces has long been among the top complaint from foreign visitors to the country , and it’s an issue that exists even in the most densely developed parts of Tokyo. In recent years, there’s been a noticeable increase in the amount of litter to be seen in the city’s most heavily touristed areas, including Akihabara. ▼ A pile of trash on the sidewalk in Akihabara in January of this year Using funds from the municipal government’s Tokyo Green Up Action subsidy program, Chiyoda Ward, which Akihabara is part of, has acquired 22 SmaGO “smart trash cans” from Tokyo-based tech company Forcetec . Fittingly for Akihabara’s image as a high-tech part of town, these receptacles are actually public trash compactors , using solar power to condense their contents down to one-fifth of their original size. They can also utilize a cloud network to inform maintenance workers of how full the bins currently are, allowing for more efficient coordination of trash pickups. ▼ As is usually the case in Japan, different types of trash go in different containers, so make sure to sort your stuff before you toss it in. The SmaGO trash cans went into service at 10 locations in Akihabara, clustered around Akihabara Station (秋葉原駅 in the map below) and along Chuo-dori (中央通り) , the major shopping street in the neighborhood. The move follows new ordinances requiring more publicly accessible trash cans, and stricter penalties for not using them, which recently went into effect across town in the Shibuya neighborhood . Both districts’ responses to increasing amounts of litter do make one feel a little sad that the current crop of visitors evidently isn’t as concerned with Japan’s customary etiquette norm of carrying your trash home with you if there’s no public place to dispose of it, but hopefully the new initiatives will result in a return to cleaner streets. title: Why people in Japan hardly ever say “sayonara,” and what they say instead
summary: Everyone knows that sayonara means goodbye in Japanese, but goodbye in Japan doesn’t always mean you need to say it. You don’t have to be an anime otaku, foodie with a penchant for matcha and wagyu, or obsessive linguistics enthusiast that know that sayonara means “goodbye” in Japanese. Like loco in Spanish and merci in French, […]
details: Everyone knows that sayonara means goodbye in Japanese, but goodbye in Japan doesn’t always mean you need to say it . You don’t have to be an anime otaku, foodie with a penchant for matcha and wagyu, or obsessive linguistics enthusiast that know that sayonara means “goodbye” in Japanese . Like loco in Spanish and merci in French, sayonara is one of those words that’s so well known internationally that it’s widely understood even by people without any personal connection to its home-country culture. And yet, living in Japan, you’ll very rarely hear anyone actually say sayonara (unless you happen to be in a pre-college school, where students of such ages say it to their teachers at the end of the school day). As a matter of fact, when someone did say it to us the other day, it was startling, even if it was also very appropriate to the specific circumstances that was taking place. But wait, if sayonara isn’t a commonly used phrase, how do people in Japan end conversations? Does one person just wander off once they think the topic has run its course, and the value that Japanese culture places on tacit understanding means that you’re just supposed to infer that the other person said goodbye to you inside their heart? ▼ Wait, Linguistics Samurai! I still had something I needed to tell you! Nope. Japanese actually has several other phrases that take sayonara’s place in the vast majority of daily situations . Let’s take a look at a few, and then circle back to why sayonara usually isn’t used. One of the most common ways to say goodbye when speaking to friends or peers in social situations is ja , which means “if” or “then.” That might seem like a pretty random choice of vocabulary, but there is a logical reason for it, which is that it’s a shortened version of sore ja , meaning “if it’s like that,” or, rendered more naturally in English “in that case” or “well then.” In this situation, sore ja is itself a pared-down version of phrases such as sore ja, kore de kaerimasu (“well then, I’m heading home”), sore ja, ikanakya ” (“well then, I’ve got to get going”), and the like. But if you don’t want to get into the nitty-gritty of why you’re saying goodbye, Japanese social norms allow you to opt out of the explanation and just say “ ja .” Used completely by itself, though, ja can sound a little curt, so to make it a little cordial the all-purpose emphasizer ne , or na among male speakers, is often tacked onto the end. Speaking of adding things after ja, another option for that is mata , the Japanese word for “again.” In this case, it’s included as an abbreviation of things such as mata aimashou (“let’s get together again [sometime]”) or mata ashita (“[see you] again tomorrow”). And to multiply our options even further, if you want to sound a little more polished and polite, you can replace ja with dewa , a more formal word with the same meaning. Mixing and matching these elements will give you all sorts of common ways of saying “goodbye” in Japanese that you’ll hear much, much more frequently than sayonara, such as: ● ja / ja ne / ja na ● dewa ● sore ja / sore dewa ● mata / mata ne / mata na ● sore ja, mata / sore ja, mata ne / sore ja, mata na ● dewa, mata ne / dewa, mata na There are two other Japanese phrases which also don’t translate literally as “goodbye” but regularly get used where we’d say that in English. One of them is otsukarasama desu , which, as we’ve discussed before , more or less means “you must be tired,” but which is commonly said between coworkers when going home at the end of the day, since you’ve both put in a full day of work. Similarly, if you’re going home while someone else is still working, the custom is to tell them osaki ni shitsurei shimasu , meaning “excuse me for going home before you,” which can be shortened down to just osaki ni if you’re on friendly terms with one another. But even knowing all that, sayonara does still mean “goodbye,” so why isn’t it said very often? Because sayonara has a very weighty nuance to it, so much so that it’s mainly used for situations where it’s not just goodbye, but possibly goodbye forever , or at the very least where there’s a very real possibility that you’ll never meet again. ▼ Hearing “sayonara” at the end of a first date is a strong sign that there’s not going to be a second. Because of that, sayonara isn’t something classmates say to each other after grabbing ramen together. It’s what they might say to each other at graduation if they’re all going off to different colleges and there’s no real guarantee they’re going to meet up again. You wouldn’t say sayonara to your coworker Tanaka-san when you clock out on a Friday evening, but you might say it to him at his going away party before his permanent transfer to an overseas office. ▼ If your coworker walks out of the office while waving and saying “Sayonara!”, there’s a good chance she just quit. In other words, when someone does tell you sayonara, it tends to stick with you, because it’s a sign of parting that might be permanent. When someone said it to us the other day, it was a bittersweet moment, so who did we hear it from? The workers at Cold Stone in the city of Kamakura, the very last branch of the chain in all of east Japan , which we visited for one last ice cream treat shortly before it closed on October 31. While he was waiting for his order, our reporter Mr. Sato briefly chatted with the staff about the shop shutting down , and when they handed him his ice cream, they told him thank you, and also “sayonara.” This is Cold Stone’s second time to leave east Japan, and it wouldn’t be a shock if the company decides not to ever take a third shot at it, and that situation was reflected in the employees’ choice of words. Now, none of this means that there’s a taboo against saying sayonara, or that it’s an old-fashioned phrase that feels out of place in the modern world. Sayonara does, though, carry a lot of emotional significance, so it’s a special phrase for special circumstance

title: Tokyo cracks down on Airbnb-style rentals with new laws limiting operator days and more
summary: With tourists’ and residents’ feelings about minpaku racing in opposite directions, wards add new local ordinances onto national laws. “Short-term private vacation lodging” is a bit of a mouthful, and while “Airbnb-style rentals” is more concise, it singles out just one company in what’s become a rapidly expanding sector of traveler accommodations. So today, let’s […]
details: With tourists’ and residents’ feelings about minpaku racing in opposite directions, wards add new local ordinances onto national laws . “Short-term private vacation lodging” is a bit of a mouthful, and while “Airbnb-style rentals” is more concise, it singles out just one company in what’s become a rapidly expanding sector of traveler accommodations. So today, let’s just call them “minpaku,” the term used in Japanese to describe rentals for travelers that weren’t originally zoned or constructed as hotels. Minpaku have been rapidly rising in popularity over the past few years. While the idea of staying in a converted home while on vacation has limited appeal to most Japanese travelers, foreign tourists have shown plenty of enthusiasm for minpaku, especially when coming to Japan in a group of friends or family members who want more communal space for their party than conventional hotels offer. That growing popularity with foreign tourists has simultaneously made minpaku’s presence increasingly unwelcome among local Japanese residents, however, and new ordinances mean that all 23 central wards of Tokyo have now introduced additional rules restricting or limiting their operation, including new bans on accepting guests on weekdays . Houses and apartments are built very close to one another in Japan’s residential neighborhoods. and that creates a sort of etiquette-deterrence situation between long-term residents. The close proximity means that any excess noise or trash generated by one neighbor is likely to affect everyone around them, and vice versa, so residents generally try to stay quiet and clean as a show of mutual consideration, with the baseline tacit agreement of “I won’t cause problems for you, and you won’t cause problems for me.” The importance of maintaining polite long-term relationships within the community doesn’t apply to short-term renters, though, who’ll probably be gone in a few days’ time, and far too often ill-mannered minpaku guests party noisily late into the night, litter in the common-use areas of the buildings they stay in and on the surrounding streets, and otherwise. Minpaku lodgings in Japan started off as a bit of a cottage industry, and the sector managed to build up significant momentum before widespread regulatory measures were put in place. Under the Private Lodging Business Law, minpaku are not allowed to accept guests for more than 180 nights in a calendar year, but many local municipalities have placed additional regulations on top of that. Most recently, Tokyo’s Kita Ward became the city’s 23rd ward to pass its own. As of January 7, Kita Ward will ban the opening of new minpaku in residential areas in which the homeowner is not present when guests are staying in the unit . Requiring the homeowner to be present should, theoretically, increase the minpaku operator’s connection, and personal responsibility, to the surrounding community, creating an accessible contact point for complaints from neighbors or regulatory enforcement by the ward, while discouraging management by remote companies whose facelessness makes it easier for them to ignore grievances. ▼ It’s harder for management to brush off complaints when they have to deal with them in-person. Tokyo’s Taito Ward is also tightening restrictions on minpaku. As of October 1, no new minpaku within the ward will be allowed to accept guests on weekdays, and no new minpaku of any kind will be allowed to open in parts of the ward which are zoned for residential-use only . Taito is also taking action against four minpaku owners who collectively operate eight units within the ward . By law, minpaku operators are required to submit reports on a minpaku’s number of guests and nights in operation every two months, but the owners filed no reports at all for the eight properties for the period between December of 2025 and May of 2026. Taito is now giving the owners approximately three weeks to submit the required documents, and says that failure to do so will result in the owners’ names being publicly announced, followed by forced closures of the minpaku if the non-compliance continues. Other parts of Tokyo are going even farther in their attempts to address residents’ growing irritation at minpaku. Shinjuku Ward, for example, is looking to add legislation that would not only designate areas within it as off-limits for new minpaku, but which would also force currently existing minpaku within them to shut down . In total, Tokyo’s 23 central wards account for roughly 40 percent of all the minpaku in Japan, so it’s likely that other cities will be watching the effectiveness of these countermeasures very closely, and possibly basing their future policies on them in an effort to stave off resident complaints before any such friction with minpaku operators/guests occurs. title: Japanese viewers of Godzilla Minus Zero angered by unusual number of restroom goers
summary: Godzilla films are famous for their subtlety and require complete concentration. Culture Day in Japan was on 3 November, and what better way to celebrate culture than by watching the latest Godzilla film, Godzilla Minus Zero? It was a thought held by many, as the monster movie drew in an amazing 910 million yen (US$5.8M) […]
details: Godzilla films are famous for their subtlety and require complete concentration. Culture Day in Japan was on 3 November, and what better way to celebrate culture than by watching the latest Godzilla film, Godzilla Minus Zero ? It was a thought held by many, as the monster movie drew in an amazing 910 million yen (US$5.8M) on its opening day alone, breaking the record for a live-action film in Japan. However, while the film itself has been incredibly well-received by critics and audiences alike, some moviegoers in Japan complained about their viewing experience . The biggest beef of all was that too many people were getting up to go to the restroom during the film. One post by a social media user said they had an aisle seat during the movie and shortly into it, people had started going to the bathroom one after another, ruining their ability to get into the story. This might just sound like a single oversensitive reaction to this sort of thing, but the post generated significant discussion, with a majority of people agreeing. Others also reported an inordinate number of people going to hit the head during their screenings of Godzilla Minus Zero (or Godzilla -0.0 as it’s known in Japan), including head counts they took during the film. It was enough to make me wonder if I was the weird one for paying absolutely no mind to other people going in and out of the theater in the many movies I’ve seen over the years. There were a few comments to the contrary, saying that complaining about such a thing was going overboard. But there were many more people talking about how hard it was for them to fight the urge to pee towards the end of the movie, which, by the way, includes sitting through the entire credits. That is expected behavior among many moviegoers in Japan , not in the hopes of seeing additional scenes, but purely out of respect for the people who made the film. I’d probably stop short of saying this is “Japanese culture” per se, but it definitely appears to be a prevailing sentiment here. To help get a sense of how people feel about this stuff, here’s a wide sampling of reactions to the situation, covering a range of opinions. “When I saw it, no one went to the bathroom, but when the end credits started, a bunch of people got up right away to leave.” “I think once that first person goes, everyone else feels like it’s okay, and the floodgates open.” “I heard someone call the movie Godzilla vs King Ghidorah vs The Urge to Pee, lol.” “A lot of people got up from their seats here too.” “That’s the problem with blockbuster movies. They draw in people who don’t usually go to the movies.” “When I saw it, the same people went in and out like six or seven times during the movie.” “There was a crazy number of people going to the bathroom!” “I was holding it in so long, it came out like a blast of atomic breath when I finally went.” “Everyone had good manners when I saw it in Wakayama.” “I saw two adults and one child get up during the movie, but no one got up during the credits.” “You should just let it slide. Holding it in isn’t good for you.” “That’s why I always watch on IMAX when possible. The screen is so big you can barely see anyone walking in front of it.” “This is why I never go to movies. Some people might have medical issues, you know?” “I get that it can’t be helped, but someone got up behind me, and I felt bad for all the people that person walked in front of.” “Seriously? Calling people out just for using the restroom? I think etiquette is going in a weird direction.” “I saw Street Fighter and had to go early on. I held it in right to the end of the credits, but it was really close.” “Soooooo many people went to the restrooms. And during one of the scenes where a character laughed, some brat in the row behind me started laughing too. Shut the hell up !” “Yeah, there were tons of people. I wonder why that is.” Regardless of people’s feelings about the situation, the one objective observation here is that an inordinate number of people do seem to be going to the restroom during Godzilla Minus Zero specifically . It’s a bit of a lengthy movie, clocking in at 135 minutes, but some mention that the number of people ducking out for a moment well exceeded that of lengthier movies such as the 172-minute-long The Odyssey . There were numerous theories as to why this is. One was that Godzilla , which dates back to the 1950s, tends to attract an older demographic who may lack the firm bladder control that the youth enjoys. The other is that the fact that a major commercial film opening on a public holiday brought in an inordinate number of people who weren’t “true movie buffs,” or perhaps just decided to see it in on a whim without planning their hydration accordingly. By the way, according to many of the comments, a popular way to suppress the urge to urinate before watching a movie is to eat Bontan Ame candies or daifuku , the latter of which are little snacks made of sweet bean paste covered in mochi. There’s no science to back this up, but who am I to deny people their placebos? There’s also a suspicion that a lot of people didn’t even leave to use a toilet. It could have been that some people weren’t prepared for the scenes of destruction depicted in the film, which can often resemble actual natural disasters and hit close to home for more than a few people in Japan. Regardless of the cause, it seems the one thing we can learn from this is that when watching a movie in Japan, the safe bet is to sit perfectly still and quiet until the very last bit of footage hits the silver screen to avoid the silent wrath and judgmental stares of those around you. details: The Straw Hat Pirates have dropped anchor in Los Angeles . Last month we got word that America would be getting its first-ever One Piece specialty store , and that the wait for it to open wouldn’t be very long. And while it was exciting for fans to look at the concept art for the One Piece Mugiwara Store Los Angeles, now that the shop is actually open we can see what the real thing looks like! November 6 was the grand opening date for the store, which is located at the Westfield Century City shopping center in Los Angeles. Representatives from One Piece animation rights holder Toei and Sony were on hand, as was Japanese professional soccer player Maya Yoshida, who has been playing for Major League Soccer’s Los Angeles Galaxy since 2023. The real star power here though, of course, comes from the characters of the series, and there’s a three-meter (9.8-foot) tall statue of Luffy in his Gear 5 guise standing at the center of the shop , plus plenty of wanted posters of the Straw Hat Pirates posted inside, as shown by Yoshida here. Chopper also gets a special “waverider Chopper” design just for the L.A. shop, showing him surfing the waters presumably just off the California coast. Fittingly for fashion-conscious L.A., there are a lot of exclusive apparel items on offer… …but this being a proper otaku-oriented retailer means that the shelves are also amply stocked with things such as figures and collected manga volumes too. Coolest of all, the One Piece Mugiwara Store Los Angeles isn’t a limited-time, pop-up event, but a permanent place for fans to gather, just like the L.A. area’s recently opened Studio Ghibli specialty shop .
